speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask leave to move the adjournment of the house, arising out of the report in the morning papers with respect to the incredible piece of legislation introduced yesterday in the Ontario legislature-

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PROPOSED ONTARIO LEGISLATION

speechtext:
-by the Conservative government. I ask leave, therefore, to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond (Mr. Prittie), the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely the introduction by the Ontario government of legislation which would destroy the principles of Magna Carta and the bill of rights, and as a result would seriously undermine the long standing principles upon which our democratic system is based.
In doing so, Mr. Speaker, I think it is vitally important that this body today register its views on this piece of legislation, so that the government of Ontario may be well aware of the seriousness with which we view this type of activity. Having served as counsel before the royal commission on crime in Ontario. I am well aware of the problem they are trying to solve; but it seems to me the solution being proposed is far too drastic and far too dangerous to be permitted to take place in a democratic society.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will consider this matter as one of grave urgency. It is important that parliament express its views immediately before any further action is taken by the Ontario government. Never to my knowledge has such a drastic piece of legislation been proposed, and unless this house today immediately registers its views there will be no further opportunity to make our views known before the government of Ontario proceeds to enact this legislation.

maintopic: "HANSARD" DESIGNATION OF LANGUAGE SPOKEN BY MEMBERS

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: "HANSARD" DESIGNATION OF LANGUAGE SPOKEN BY MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I may say it has to do with a matter which I have discussed with the editor of Hansard, who shares my concern. I raise it now in the hope that other hon. members may have suggestions to make to meet the problem.
Since the English edition of Hansard was revised so that it appears entirely in English, it has become necessary to indicate whether a member's words are recorded in the language in which he spoke or whether they are a translation. As hon. members know, there appear in Hansard repeatedly the words "translation" and "text". Yesterday, for example, you, sir, intervened at a certain point in our proceedings which were being conducted in French. Since you spoke at that point in English, the word "text" appears just over your words as reported. We know what this means, but it almost looks as though you were handed a text of what to say.

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire
In my own case, I have on occasion made a speech-and I believe hon. members know that I do not use a manuscript; frequently I do not even use any notes-following an hon. member who has spoken in French, and on such an occasion the word "text" appears over the report of what I have said. I suggest that this gives rise to a false impression; it is something we should make an effort to have corrected. I know the editor of Hansard is concerned about it, and I hope somebody may come up with a suggestion as to how the possibility of misunderstanding might be removed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first part of my remarks yesterday, I mentioned the financial position of this country, of its boards, corporations and intermediate bodies, and I stressed their rather disastrous position, because of the huge size of the federal, provincial, municipal, industrial, individual and school board debts.
Mr. Speaker, I also mentioned that the federal government had ceased to be an administrative or legislative body to become a loan institution: loans to municipalities, farmers, students, business, Indians, immigrants, veterans, and so on.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to dwell a little on loans to students, simply to congratulate those most concerned in the matter, that is the students themselves, who have the greatest need of those loans, but having realized that this government bill was a direct impingement on the educational field, which comes under provincial jurisdiction, they had the courage to oppose and refuse those federal loans. I shall quote the words of Mr. Robert Bazinet, vice president of the general student association of the University of Montreal, who, speaking on behalf of that association, said:
If Ottawa offers loans to students (although this field is reserved to the provinces) it means they are not short of funds.
That is the paradox nowadays; the federal government is prepared to offer money to


students, a matter not within its jurisdiction, but is neglectful of its responsibilities in various other matters.
Mr. Speaker, what is the present economic situation in this country?
It is realized that our industries, our manufacturing plants, our natural resources are in the hands of foreign financial interests in a proportion of 70 to 75 per cent while, on the other hand, Canadian citizens are merely employees, in view of foreign control of our industries and natural resources. That is the situation in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, foreign interests control our natural resources and our industries, while Canadians are merely wage earners.
What is the economic situation in this country?
We have an increasing number of bankruptcies. With the spreading of automation, there is little job security. Faced with such a situation, our governments do nothing to provide new jobs.
What is the real situation in this country, Mr. Speaker?
We just found out that our farmers, at least eastern farmers, have an average annual income of $1,800. But for tens of thousands of farmers, that average annual income barely comes to $1,200.
We are talking about unemployment, Mr. Speaker, but figures in this regard have been distorted. Only people not receiving unemployment insurance benefits are now included in the figure, although there are as many if not more Canadian citizens who are not taking advantage of such benefits and have to be satisfied with social assistance benefits. Therefore, figures supplied by the Department of Finance are basically false since the actual data should include those receiving unemployment insurance benefits or social assistance benefits, for the latter too are unemployed.
Such is the true situation in Canada; there are more unemployed than reported, because relevant figures are concealed.
A professor from the University of Montreal, Mr. Andre Patry, stated recently:
Foreign investments in Canada are now close to $25 billion and 80 per cent of them are American. They represent 60 per cent of the national income in our country;
Sixty per cent of our national income is controlled by foreign interests.
And Professor Patry added:
In the United States, foreign investments have never exceeded 15 per cent of the national income.
Here is another quotation, Mr. Speaker:
Professor Hans Selye, directer of the institute of experimental medicine at the University of Montreal

has just stated: "Fifty per cent of my students who have obtained their doctor's degree at the University of Montreal are now working abroad".
Fifty per cent of the students who have obtained their doctor's degree in experimental medicine from the University of Montreal are working abroad.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) told us the other day that unemployment in Canada is due to a shortage of skilled labour.
As a matter of fact, our skilled labour, especially skilled workmen who engaged in research and obtained university degrees, are unable to make a living in Canada; that is why half of them go and seek jobs in other countries.
The latest brief of the Canadian federation of labour unions reads as follows:
Industrial research takes place in the United States. Such a procedure deprives us of our own technology and drains our country of its scientists for the benefit of the United States.
Such is the economic situation in our country. Canada is unable to provide jobs for its scientists who have to seek employment elsewhere and, as a result, our scientists are unemployed in Canada.
Yesterday, I had the opportunity to outline a particular situation in the house, namely the national debt, as well as the fact that Canada is getting everybody into debt.
That outline seemed to rouse somewhat the imagination of members of the house, since they asked us to suggest a solution to those problems.
This solution can be found through an adjustment of our Canadian monetary system. At present in that field the situation is such, that at all levels, the government as well as individuals are still at the mercy of the credit controllers of our country.
Those who control money and credit in our country govern its expansion, as well as the governments, the industries and the people. Such a situation still prevails at this time.
That is why in Canada, government and individuals alike are crawling in the front of credit controllers so that they might carry out their operations.
I mentioned yesterday that the debt in our country is higher than the money resources or money supply in circulation. Why? Because the credit controllers want to keep the government in bondage, and the whole country under their thumb in order to control them better and make them act according to their own sweet will.
I am asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) what would happen if tomorrow the federal government creditors were to ask him to pay off his debts? The Minister
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire of Finance would not be able, even by scraping all the money in the country, to find enough to pay them off.
Therefore, he would have to sell the properties of all the citizens of Canada to be able to pay the debt of the federal government. In the circumstances, where is the security of our industries, our businesses and our people?
I see that one of our hon. friends opposite is yapping. I ask him what he would do if the Minister of Finance told him to sell his own property to pay the debts of the country or the government? He would be the first to protest strongly-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He would stop being a Liberal then.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And he is only one man. But the situation is the same for each and every Canadian citizen.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is someone who does not seem to know much because he never rises from his seat-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some unknown member.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -I cannot even mention his riding, Mr. Speaker, because I do not know it. He never rises; we have never heard him say a word.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here is the solution. Let us take away from some individuals the control of our country's credit and give it back to a sovereign state which will have full use of its money through the Bank of Canada. At the present time, the chartered banks control the country and have only one aim, to make profits out of the government and the public accounts by creating money to lend it later to the government and the public bodies. Those people also make profits and become wealthy on our taxes and contributions. That is the first disgraceful thing which it is imperative to denounce and which has to be tackled in the first place.
We are, and always will be, a colony from an economic point of view, as long as we have no sovereign government actually controlling credit in this country.
Once the government controls its own credit, the whole country, industry and every individual will benefit because by exerting such control, the government will not only seek profits, but also develop this country and ensure the well-being of each and every citizen in Canada.
This is the solution to the problem: take over the control of what I would call the most important instrument of development

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire lor this country, that is control of money, control of credit, which the government relinquished to a few profiteers who are making money by keeping the people in abject poverty.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words regarding federal-provincial tax relations.
I took note of some figures indicating the chief expenses of the federal and provincial governments, to prove that at this time, the provinces have precedence over the federal government. If anybody asks what are this country's needs at the present, the answer is: education. Now what does the federal government spend for education?
The last relevant figures-for 1963-were published somewhat belatedly as usual, in the Canada Year Book 1963-64. Those statistics show that, in 1960, the federal government appropriated $64,480,000 for education, whereas the provinces and the school boards which come under the municipalities spent $1,513,945,000, that is 26 times as much.
This clearly shows that the provinces did more than their share in that respect. The provinces have larger needs, but they have had more expenditures.
The second main item at this time, among our priority requirements, is national health. What were in 1960, the federal government expenditures for national health? They amounted to $267,222,000 while the provinces and municipalities had total expenditures of $574,128,000, that is twice as much.
And for transportation, the federal government spent $104,964,000, while provinces and municipalities spent $1,070 million, that is ten times as much.
As far as the protection of individuals and properties is concerned, the federal government spent $79,185,000 while the provinces spent $308,429,000, that is five times more.
Well, Mr. Speaker, for those four items, the most important ones in the social life of this country, the provinces and municipalities spent a total of $3,526,877,000, while the federal government spent $515,843,000, that is seven times less than the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a distinguished member of our press gallery qualified the budget with a simple but very proper word when he said:
In short, it is a.. .reasonable budget.
This budget is no more interesting than the uneventful life of a happy family. The minister puts the emphasis on youth by encouraging studies. The budget will also help boost the economy in designated areas. But with regard to the financial situation in our country, the budget reflects prosperity and there is nothing mysterious about that. Under the direction of an industrious and alert minister, the only thing Canadians have to do is to work and reap the fruits of their labour.
Mr. Speaker, I know that, traditionally, the budget debate gives hon. members the opportunity to express their views on any point of this important document, which relates to the immediate needs of their own riding.
If I somewhat deviate from normal practice today, it is because for nearly a year now I have had the privilege of serving Canada as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). That appointment entailed a certain amount of work, but it opened my eyes, as a citizen of Quebec, to the major role played by crown corporations in our province.
In many quarters, criticism has been voiced recently against the activity of the federal government and of its corporations as regards the past, the present and the future of Quebec. However, one merely has to examine the facts with an open mind, objectively and without partisanship, to see that there is a great difference between such allegations and reality.
As parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport, I have been in a position to check the facts. Today, I should like to report my findings to my Quebec colleagues on both sides of the house. I shall speak mostly of the Canadian economy and national unity. If, nowadays, one can state publicly without any supporting evidence that separatism is possible socially, politically and economically, it might be appropriate to remind the people that figures also have a meaning. The budget gives the government's sources of income and it indicates that federal funds are used not only for the administration of the country,

but also to carry out the program of the government, whose outstanding objective is national unity.
During the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the majority of speakers have referred to the matter of national unity. It is probably because the centennial of confederation is just around the corner and also because there is in Quebec a general awakening of nationalism resulting in vocal extremist movements where sentiments take precedence over reason.
Moderation when making public statements is the advice I gave to all my constituents at the beginning of 1964. I feel that in this way right-minded Canadians will find a solution to the problems facing national unity.
A couple of weeks ago during a debate over television on the issue of Quebec claims inside or outside confederation, one of the English speaking panelists exclaimed in an outburst of impatience:
Remember 1759.
A good answer would be: Remember 1812, remember Chateauguay, when the stand taken by French Canada made possible, through the constitutional acts which followed, the founding of our great country. For French Canadians, it meant reconciliation and hope.
And this leads us to take stock of the centennial of confederation. As far as relations between French and English Canadians are concerned, there is certainly a resolute movement in Quebec to affirm in the face of Canada and of the world its cultural heritage, its will to share in the economy and its new awareness as a social group. If one attempts to find solutions to the problems which jeopardize our relations, one must take those elements into account.
And there must also be understanding from English Canada which, in this North American continent where the majority of people speak the same language, is not faced with the obligation of creating favourable conditions to ensure its own survival. However, this is no reason why we, French Canadians, should refuse to engage in a dialogue and deceive ourselves to the point of failing to recognize the cultural, economic and social advantages that our federal system has meant to our group.
I should like to restrict myself today to a single example of this principle, namely the economic contribution of the C.N.R. to the provinces of Quebec. All federal crown corporations were originally set up to ensure the well-being of all Canadians and of every province.
Although I intend to limit my remarks to the contribution made by the Canadian National Railways to the province of Quebec,
The Budget-Mr. Cantin needless to say the Canadian National Railways have also contributed to the development of every other section of the country. This is self-evident. But some people tried so hard to minimize that contribution to the province of Quebec that it may be advisable to try to show the true importance of this contribution to our province. I wish more particularly to point out that the government of Canada has nevertheless done something, and often a great deal for each of the provinces, including Quebec. When listening to some extremists who speak out of turn, we get the impression that Quebec was only a victim in confederation, whereas even if everything is not perfect, there are nevertheless assets which an objective mind cannot and must not ignore.
The Canadian National Railways play an important part in the economy of the prov-vince of Quebec.
In 1962, the C.N.R. numbered in the province 21,994 employees, whose salaries and wages represented over $120 million.
These salaries and wages alone represent a strong measure of support for Quebec's economy. Nevertheless, they represent only part of the contribution of the system to the general development.
Besides salaries and wages, the C.N.R. paid out in 1962 $1,443,054 in sickness and social security insurance benefits, in addition to $595,079 under the workmen's compensation act, and $5,412,927 to its Quebec retired employees or their dependants.
During 1962 alone, the purchases made by the C.N.R. in the province of Quebec amounted to $89 million.
The Queen Elizabeth hotel alone, which belongs to the C.N.R. and which is operated by Hilton of Canada Ltd., cost $7,125,000 in expenses of all kinds including salaries, new equipment and material.
We must not forget taxes either. In 1962, the C.N.R. paid the province and its municipalities $4,646,680 in sales taxes, land taxes and others.
Since the war, the railway has built more mileage of tracks in Quebec than in all the other provinces combined. That permitted the development of Quebec's natural resources accordingly.
The first project was the 39-mile long branch line which connects Barraute and Beattyville since 1949. Over the last years, the C.N.R. has added 161 miles of tracks between Beattyville and Chibougamau, another 133 miles between Chibougamau and St. Felicien and, more recently, it inaugurated a new line 61 miles long to Mattagami. This is a total of 394 miles costing $46.5 million.

The Budget-Mr. Cantin
The rolling stock-railway cars and engines- involves, oi course, on the part of the railway company, continuous expenditures which have become a heavier burden. Since the end of the war, the C.N.R. initiated a comprehensive program so as to modernize its equipment, including dieselization. Since 1946 the cost involved in this program, as far as the Canadian lines are concerned, amounts to $798,740,103 and almost 44 per cent of this amount, this is $353,083,637 have been paid to Quebec industries.
During that same year, Quebec dockyards built five ships for C.N.R. services. Included in those ships, was the Abegweit ferry operating between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island; it was built in the dockyards of Marine Industries Limited in Sorel. Canadian Vickers Limited built the William Carson operating a shuttle service between Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, and Davie Shipbuilding Limited constructed the Bluenose which now carries passengers and automobiles between Nova Scotia and the state of Maine. Those ships have cost $23.5 million.
The inauguration of the Queen Elizabeth hotel in 1958, the largest in Canada, was one of the greatest achievements of the C.N.R. which has spent $25.7 million to build and equip the hotel, the only one it has built in the past 20 years.
It is the fourth building to be erected on C.N.R. property in the area of Central station, in the heart of Montreal, and the third built by the company in that section.
The first building to be erected was the Central station which is still the most functional of the larger passenger stations in North America and which will become even more important when the C.N.R. has completed the construction of the huge building complex now under way or in the project stage. Built at a cost of $27.5 million, the station was inaugurated in 1943. In 1950, the C.N.R. completed the construction of the international aviation building at a cost of $4 million; it houses the head offices of various aviation companies and international air transport associations. The third was the Terminal Centre building erected by private interests at a cost of $4 million.
The fifth building in that group, the new C.N.R. headquarters which the staff has occupied since May 1961, cost $17.5 million.
The C.N.R. invited private enterprise to share in the development of its remaining real property located south of Lagauchetiere street.
The development of this land has raised such great interest in financial circles that Dorchester street, between Windsor street and Beaver Hall Hill, is destined to become the

most dynamic cultural and business section in North America and the most remarkable architectural achievement on this continent.
Knowing perfectly well how important was the site of the Central station and the property around it, the C.N.R. wish to promote its logical development in co-operation with private enterprise. It did so jointly with Webb and Knapp (Canada) Ltd., which drew up a master plan for the whole 23 acres and leased the seven acres located north of Central station, where the said company built the complex called "Place Ville-Marie".
That group includes the largest office building in Canada, multi-level parking, an esplanade, stores, restaurants, theatres. The project cost about $105 million.
The largest electronically-controlled hump yard in the world was inaugurated in Montreal in 1961. It cost the C.N.R. $32 million and helps greatly to speed up and improve the services for shippers and buyers of merchandise in Montreal and elsewhere in Quebec. The C.N.R. spent some $17 million to provide for a detour from Victoria bridge in Montreal, following the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. The main by-pass which at present goes through the town of Lachine cost $5 million. It eliminates a series of level crossings and thus provides an access road on the western side of the hump yard.
The C.N.R.'s industrial development service has played a major role in the establishment of enterprises in Quebec. In 1958, the C.N.R. built a five-mile branch line at Pointe Claire, near Montreal, to add 1,406 acres of land to an industrial district. Sixty nine sites were sold and 35 industries were built up. There are still approximately 923 acres left for the industrial complex which the C.N.R. is putting up, six acres of which will be occupied by a $75 million building that will be known as Place Bonaventure.
In 1959, at Candiac, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, opposite Montreal, the company built a spur line so as to permit the development of a 550-acre area suitable for industry. Six large concerns bought 100 acres of land along the railroad and many smaller firms settled there.
The railway company extended an industrial branch line from Leduc boulevard, in Montreal island's eastern section, to serve the B.P. Refinery Canada Limited Company. Later on, the C.N.R. used this branch line to allow the expansion of another industrial area of a thousand acres in Ville d'Anjou. As a result of those projects initiated by the C.N.R., some industries are now provided with private railroad lines.
The C.N.R. advised a great number of Quebec municipalities on the choice of sites suitable for setting up industries and laid

out the most suitable railway routes. Petite Riviere, St. Romuald, Sherbrooke, St. Eus-tache, St. Eustache on the Lake, St. Jerome, Mattagami, Chambly, Valleyfield, Varennes and Vercheres have thus new industrial areas, the size of which varies between 50 and
1,000	acres.
The Varennes-Contrecoeur-Tracy area seems assured of a prosperous industrial future because of the tremendous commercial development initiated by the Canadian National Railways.
The increase in the Canadian National Railways facilities and services is parallel to the Quebec industrial development. For instance, in 1962, the company's industrial development department contributed to the establishment of 55 industries-which became customers-by building 12 i miles of private branch lines and tracks in addition to the new C.N.R. tracks built in Quebec.
The C.N.R. and the C.P.R. have installed and are operating jointly a microwave system which enabled the cities of Sherbrooke, Three Rivers, Quebec, Rimouski, Jonquiere and Carleton to be linked to the C.B.C. French television network. The C.N.R. telecommunications have also set up other facilities to connect through microwaves Saint Arsene and Riviere du Loup, thus enabling the C.B.C. French network (Montreal-Moncton) to extend its services to a new station of the T.V. network established in Riviere du Loup.
The C.N.R. telecommunications have already connected cities such as Montreal, Sherbrooke, Chicoutimi, Granby, Three Rivers, Noranda, Quebec, Thetford Mines and Senne-terre to its Telex system. At the end of June 1963, there was in Quebec alone, approximately a thousand subscribers who could obtain instantaneous and printed communication with 9,700 other customers in Canada and in the United States.
The Canadian National Railways have recently set up in Montreal, for the first time in Canada, a new semi-automatic system for rerouting telegrams to speed up their delivery.
In 1962 the C.N.R. telecommunications took a significant step ahead when in co-operation with the C.P.R., the development of a Mont-real-Vancouver microwave system was undertaken at a cost of $36 million. The gigantic undertaking provided for the RCA Victor Company of Montreal a $12 million contract for the purchase of electronic material.
In order to provide the national defence department with telecommunication facilities, the C.N.R. invested $5 million for the development of repeater stations in Chibougamau and Miquelon, and for the extension of the C.N.T. building in Senneterre.
I only reviewed the C.N.R.'s major achievements and expenditures. During the same
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin period, hundreds of smaller projects and improvements were carried out in Quebec.
To summarize, these last few years, the C.N.R.'s capital expenditures in the province of Quebec alone came to $568,460,637, while the expenditures of private corporations established on C.N.R. properties came to $677,460,637. As regards the C.N.R.'s operating expenses for the year 1962, and in the province of Quebec alone, the figure is $203,260,740.
As far as the promotion of French Canadians within the C.N.R. is concerned, I refer to the Gordon report already tabled in this house, to add that since that time, the C.N.R. has appointed a new vice president in the person of Mr. Pierre Delagrave, whose leadership and imagination were at the basis of the modernization of the C.N.R. passenger service.
We have there, I believe, somewhat of a reply to those who readily state, without proof, that separatism is possible from an economic point of view. It might be interesting to extend this study to all other federal corporations and government services. Quebec's economy would be tragically affected through the loss of those customers and services, even though the railway service would be maintained, but entirely at the expense of the people of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, figures also speak for themselves and this account of relations between French and English Canadians must be added to the historical, political, social and purely human values given to us by confederation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I take advantage of this opportunity to participate in the budget debate and cast my few pearls of wisdom before the crowded treasury benches opposite, I wish I could utter a few words of kindness to the minister. However, try as I might the best I can say of this budget is that it is not one to excite the daring and, despite the fact he waved the ministerial wand lightly over the Scotch whisky, it is hardly a budget to intoxicate the sober.
I am going to deal mainly, Mr. Speaker, with the question of trade and commerce, because it is inextricably bound up with the budget and with fiscal and financial policies. I propose to deal with this question if time permits, and I hope this does not sound like a threat, as it relates to external trade, possibly commonwealth trade and definitely domestic trade and commerce.
I must say that so far as the government's position is concerned it reminds me of something which, if it were genetically possible, would be the result of crossing the proverbial
12S6

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin ostrich with the colourful figure from Dickens, Mr. Micawber, and this creature were then to sit on the treasury benches opposite. In so far as this question of trade and commerce is concerned, the government has buried its head deep in the sand, while the winds of change blow over that part of its anatomy exposed to them; and the only words we can hear the government uttering are the immortal words of Mr. Micawber, "I do hope that something is going to turn up."
In so far as the budget relates to trade and commerce, for example, I do realize that the minister has refused to provide for any tax cuts. In doing so he has given what he thinks are proper reasons for this course, and they are recorded on page 976 of Hansard. These may be sufficient in one sense of the word, and I think they probably are. Nevertheless, sir, we cannot escape from the fact that over the next year or so the question of our foreign trade is going to be of the utmost importance. It appears likely, on the eve of this great gathering in Geneva, that there are going to be concessions made. Many nations are committed to this principle, and I do not think there can be any withdrawal from it. However, in so far as the conditions, terms and timing are concerned, these things will depend upon the negotiations, upon the skill of the negotiators and the manner in which the negotiations are conducted.
It seems to me, however, that Canada is singularly unprepared to enter into this negotiating area. If the minister had seen fit to include in his budget selective tax concessions which could have been designated and related to price reductions, this would have strengthened our position tremendously. Eventually during the course of these negotiations, which are going to progress over the next year or so, we are going to receive concessions; we are going to ask for concessions, and I am sure we are going to have to reciprocate. Manufacturers in Canada will, in all likelihood, be unable to reduce prices having in mind the failure to provide these tax cuts. There are certain indications in the budget and in the estimates that the cost of government is rising and is going to continue to rise, and the present administration gives no sign of relief in this field.
The United States has provided for tax cuts, I think in the amount of $11.5 billion for the next short period of time. There is no doubt at all that these concessions will be reflected in lower prices for many of the commodities produced by the United States with which our goods will have to compete. The minister has said that even without tax cuts there is still a comparison between the situation in the United States and the situation here. That is not good enough. We will have


to be able to face the competition which we are bound to meet from the lower prices of the American goods which are bound to follow these tax cuts. I think this is a weapon which the minister should have made use of, and I fear we may yet regret and live to rue the day that selective concessions of this kind were not included in the budget.
I now wish to make reference to the position which has been indicated with regard to Japan. On March 11 last, as recorded at page 795 of Hansard for that date, I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Is It correct.. .that the Canadian government has requested Japan to reduce its quotas on a number of commodities exported to Canada as far as 1964 is concerned.
The minister's reply was:
-negotiations are now proceeding with the Japanese government on the voluntary restraints which have been in effect for some years now. I do not think it would be appropriate for me to add anything to that at the present time.
This is obviously an admission that our government has requested Japan to reduce further the quotas, or voluntary restraints as the minister described them, which now exist. I am sure if this had not been the case the minister would have said so. I have in mind the favourable balance which now exists so far as Canada is concerned. I have just obtained information from the Department of Trade and Commerce that for 1963 total Canadian exports to Japan were in the order of $297 million, while imports from Japan to Canada were only $130 million.
I have heard all the trite arguments as to why we should ask the Japanese to permit us to enlarge our trade with them and at the same time say they must reduce their exports to us. But I think these are all specious arguments and at this particular stage, on the eve of this great international bargaining, we are guilty of a very serious omission if we engage in this dangerous exercise in international trade relations.
Some comment could also be directed to our trade relations with China. In the 1962-63 report of the Canadian wheat board covering that crop year reference is made to our agreement with the People's Republic of China, and on page 13 of the report we find this statement:
All deferred payments in connection with the above agreement-
That is, the sale of grain.
-have been honoured on or before the due date. As of July 31. 1963 the balance outstanding was $51,361,329. By September 9, 1963 this entire amount has been prepaid.
In other words our Chinese customers not only made good their payments on due dates but prepaid over $50 million well in advance

of the due dates. To me this seems to constitute an irrebuttable argument to those who have said these were not good sales, that we should not proceed with them, and that a mistake had been made. But it is simply not good enough to take this as the status quo. I think those who say our sales to China will be determined only by weather conditions and by the vicissitudes of Chinese agriculture overlook the fact that our proximity to China indicates this will be a continuing trade; but for it to be so, there must be reciprocal steps taken. We must be prepared to encourage a reasonable flow, an increasing flow, of Chinese goods into Canada. This is a suggestion which the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take into consideration, and I would hope when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) returns from his visit to China, that on a non-partisan basis he will not hesitate to make use of the information which has been obtained in that way.
I want to speak very briefly, Mr. Speaker, about the question of commonwealth trade. In doing so I support the position taken by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) who indicated that the government was entitled to be criticized for its failure to do anything about it and for taking a negative attitude. A series of articles has been appearing in the Christian Science Monitor by S. C. Leslie, formerly head of the information service of the British treasury, who has given some study to this subject following the collapse of the British efforts to enter the common market. I am not going to take the time to analyze these, but before I give some of the conclusions Mr. Leslie has arrived at I wish to say that those who either suggest or acquiesce in the view that we should write off the commonwealth of nations forget there are several things in favour of the commonwealth.
First, it is in existence. Second, it has a tradition, an experience and an accumulated knowledge derived from the participation of many nations over a long period of time. Third, it is important in its association which covers countries, peoples, races and religions all over the world, something that we will have to learn to do if we are to get along together. For that reason I think there should be every effort to make the utmost use of the commonwealth of nations now in existence. Having said that, I want to put on the record a few concrete suggestions which Mr. Leslie makes with regard to the economic aspects of the commonwealth. He says:
On the economic side, the proposals that have been responsibly put forward include (1) an export council with regional subdivisions... (2) a development council to analyse, discuss and coordinate plans for growth: (3) a commonwealth bank... (4) more collaboration in maintaining the
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin central reserves and more co-ordination of balance of payments policies among the members; (5) long term bilateral trading arrangements not involving tariff changes; (6) the adoption and active promulgation of a more ambitious program of financial and technical aid, with specific targets: (7) and finally, and in the long run perhaps the most important of all, the resolute development and extension of the network of educational links, exchanges, and assistance programs, which are part of the very fibre of the partnership: a commonwealth university has been mentioned.
I put those forward as very reasonable, very logical and very attainable objectives.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the time left to me I wish to deal with the question of domestic trade, and I wish to limit my remarks particularly to the problem which has been raised as a result of steps recently taken by the Quebec government in what I think has been improper action, both legally and otherwise, in banning the export of lumber. I shall also refer to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce today. The question may be asked, why should I bring this subject up? Well, I come from a constituency many thousands of miles away. For that reason I am probably better equipped to do it because it cannot be said I have any interest, either on behalf of myself or my constituents, in this particular aspect of what is a very serious problem.
Then I come from a constituency which has experienced precisely the same problem that I think has motivated the Quebec government to do what it has done. For years, in fact even for generations, in my area we had to sit helplessly by while primary products of agriculture and of the forest, and in addition mineral products, were extracted and taken from our district to other provinces and other countries where the final steps in processing them were completed. As a result we lost much. We lost many of our young people who saw no future in remaining in the north country, and to whom a high school graduation certificate was simply a one way ticket out of the country.
But since 1957-and I hope I am not being overly partisan when I say this-due to the policy instituted by the previous government, this has changed. I think railway history will probably be made in the not too distant future, because I am given to understand that the Great Slave railway is only a short distance from the Northwest Territories, and when it reaches there it will be the first time a railroad has been constructed to connect the Northwest Territories with the rest of Canada.
I have every sympathy for the people who were affected by this order of the Quebec government and with those who hope to benefit by it, but I submit this has to be done in a way which is within the law and

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin within the framework of our constitutional process. There is a great reservoir of understanding and sympathy for the reasonable and legitimate aspirations of the people of Quebec. This exists, I think, all over Canada and I would hate to see it spoiled by what I can only describe as occasional chauvinistic and provocative actions on the part of the government of that province.
With regard to the constitution, I am not one of those who hold that it is sacred and cannot be changed. As one hon. member said earlier, laws are made for people and people are not made to be regulated and adjusted for the convenience of laws. As a matter of fact I have on the order paper a resolution proposing what I believe to be a reasonable way of dealing with and amending the constitution and of putting before the people of this country suggestions along those lines.
But apart from other considerations, the question of trade is vital. Section 121 of the British North America Act provides for the free movement of goods between provinces. This, I submit, is the spinal cord of this confederation. If you sever that you sever everything. When we look across the Atlantic today we see the growth of a great force, economically and ultimately politically, in the common market. Many of us in this country came originally from countries in Europe which were unable to get along together in a commercial, economic or social sense. It would be most ironic if we were to disintegrate at the very time when those countries were beginning to join together. Yet this is what could happen if actions of the kind I have in mind were allowed to go unchecked.
The legislation upon which the action of Quebec is based-I understand this is an act rather than a directive-is to be found in the 1946 statutes of Quebec, chapter 25(8).
In addition to the other conditions prescribed by this act, the wood cut on the timber limits granted under its authority must be worked in the province and shall not be exported in its rough state without the authorization of the lieutenant governor in council, who may determine the reservations and conditions to which such authorization shall be subject.
Note the words "shall not be exported in its rough state". That is a prohibition of the export of a commodity produced in this particular province. What would happen if other provinces took a similar position? There would be imitation. There would be retaliation. I think of my own province of Alberta. There might be retaliation in the sense that exports from other provinces would be prohibited. Even worse, there might be retaliation in the sense of a prohibition of imports. We have an act known as the trade and

industry act under which the provincial government issues licences to manufacturers and retailers in almost all classes of trade. What would happen if as a condition of granting such licences the provincial government were to say "We will grant you a licence to manufacture and sell retail, but only on condition that you do not import from the province of Quebec any lumber, maple syrup or manufactured products of any kind". This would be precisely the same type of regulation, only in reverse.
This particular section, which is section 121 of the British North America Act, has been the subject of some judicial interpretation. The case which arose most lately, and I think the one in which the question was most fully discussed, was the case of Murphy v. C.P.R. in 1958. This, as Your Honour may remember, is the case in which a farmer sought to test the validity of the Canadian Wheat Board Act by attempting to ship some sacks of grain from the province in which he grew it to another province. Mr. Justice Rand, as reported on page 153 of Dominion Law Reports, volume 15 said:
I take section 121, apart from customs duties, to be aimed against trade regulation which is designed to place fetters upon or raise impediments to or otherwise restrict or limit the free flow of commerce across the dominion-
And again;
What is forbidden is a trade regulation that in its essence and purpose is related to a provincial boundary.
What clearer demonstration could there be of such a trade regulation than the particular section of the Quebec legislation which I have quoted? It is interesting to note that while this was placed on the statute books of Quebec in 1946, it was not enforced until recently. I think this is probably because the governments of Quebec since 1946 have had grave doubts as to its validity.
I asked the Minister of Justice in this house some time ago a question on this important subject. I asked him if he would consult with his officials and consider the validity of this particular section of the Quebec act. He has not replied. He has not answered my question, and I think that is significant. If I am wrong-and I have been wrong before; I have had many judges tell me I am wrong- I will be glad to hear it. But I think I am entitled to raise this matter. I think there is a strong suggestion in the light of what Mr. Justice Rand has said that this legislation is invalid. What is to prevent other provinces saying "Quebec is able to get away with it, why can't we?" I think the members of the government who have taken the oath as privy councillors have a duty cast upon them to examine this matter with the greatest of

care and take the action which they are required to take, despite the fact that it might be a sensitive and delicate task.
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one more particular reference to make to the subject matter with which I was dealing before one o'clock, namely the problems raised by the Quebec legislation in connection with the export of lumber. This morning my hon. friend the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for the second time raised this particular question and asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) whether he was now in a position to reply to a question he had asked about it. He obviously is also concerned. The minister, I think rather cavalierly, shrugged it off by saying, "Well, the Quebec minister in question has now issued what is in effect a clarifying statement which says he did not mean what he said the first time". The minister also referred to a news item. I have what 1 think is the news item to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred, and I find in it the following:
The spokesman-
This is the spokesman for the Quebec minister of lands and forests:
-said a statement made by Lucien Cliche, lands and forests minister, means that the department will require a cutter to get an export permit before shipping wood across the boundary to Ontario mills.
This is not any changed position; this is simply a reaffirmation of what I suggest is the offensive, repugnant provision contained in the Quebec legislation. I do not think the Minister of Trade and Commerce directed his attention this morning to this very, very grave issue. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this particular subject matter, I make this suggestion. This is such a serious matter that it should be, if it is not already, on the agenda for the federal-provincial conference. Every effort should be made by this government, in consultation with the Quebec government, to see that this provision is not enforced. I tried to get some figures as to what could possibly be involved, in terms of dollars and cents, in interprovincial freight. I found this was obviously impossible, but I also find that in terms of volume 200 million tons of freight are carried on an interprovincial basis on the railways, on ships and by trucks.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Per month, or per year?
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is per year-200 million tons. This is the very lifelood of the existence of this nation. If this small cancer is allowed to continue and to be perpetuated, I suggest that the tentacles of national trade which heretofore have largely persisted in an east and west direction will become disengaged and, seeking some nourishment, will go south of the border. If this should happen, I suggest we would cease to exist as a viable, economic unit.
I suggest therefore to the minister, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that they should do everything they can to see that this is not allowed to continue. I am never positive as to my assumptions of the law. As I said before, I have been told by judges often enough that I am not right. But I am sufficiently concerned about this to suggest that at the very least the government should see that this matter is submitted, by terms of reference, to the Supreme Court of Canada and it should not be allowed to continue to the stage where there will be retaliation and imitation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is with some trepidation that I ventured into this particular area, because I know it is sensitive. Too many people have rushed in where wiser men have feared to tread. But I feel so concerned about it that I thought it my duty to raise the matter in the way I have. Let me possibly make amends by putting on the record a statement made in 1889 by a great Canadian, a former leader of the Liberal party and a former prime minister. These words were uttered by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Quebec on June 24, 1889. May I apologize for not saying this in French. I can make shift and say words from time to time in French, but in a matter of this kind I do not think the language should be mutilated, as I am sure it would be mutilated if I attempted to say these words in French. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said this:
We are French Canadians, but our country is not confined to the territory overshadowed by the citadel of Quebec; our country is Canada...the fertile lands bordered by the bay of Fundy, the valley of the St. Lawrence, the region of the great lakes, the prairies of the west, the Rocky mountains, the lands washed by the famous ocean where breezes are said to be as sweet as the breezes of the Mediterranean. Our fellow countrymen are not only those In whose veins runs the blood of France. They are all those, whatever their race or whatever their language, whom the fortune of war, the chances of fate, or their own choice have brought among us.. .As far as I am concerned, I am a Canadian. But I told it elsewhere, and with greater pleasure I repeat here this evening, among all my fellow countrymen, the first place in my heart is for those in whose veins runs the blood of my own veins. Yet I do not hesitate to say that the rights of my fellow countrymen

The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
of different origins are as dear to me, as sacred to me, as the rights of my own race, and if it unfortunately happened that they ever were attacked I would defend them with just as much energy and vigour as the rights of my own race.
I say I: should X not say you, we all of us? Yes, we are too much the sons of France, of that generous nation which has so often shed her blood for the defence of the weak, of the oppressed, not to be ever ready to defend the rights of our fellow countrymen of different nationalities to the same extent as our own. What I claim for us is an equal share of the sun, of justice, of liberty; we have that share and have it amply; and what we claim for ourselves we are anxious to grant to others. I do not want French Canadians to domineer over anyone, nor anyone to domineer over them. Equal justice; equal rights.. .Cannot we believe that in the supreme battle here on the plains of Abraham, when the fate of arms turned against us, cannot we believe that it entered into the designs of Providence that the two races, enemies up to that time, should henceforth live in peace and harmony? Such was the inspiring cause of confederation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nothing could show better the lack of real liberalism in this government, this complete lack of concern for the needs of the people of Canada, than this budget which we are discussing at the present time. In less than two years the architect of the new Liberal look, the author of "Troubled Canada'', has been reduced to producing one of the dullest, one of the most Tory, one of the most stand pat budgets which any Canadian parliament has had to discuss. Because unemployment is somewhat down, because many Canadians are living well, the minister will have us believe that our problems have been solved. The minister is proud of the fact that he has reduced the budget deficit by one third. By doing so he has ignored the needs of the Canadian people and the promises made by his party during the election campaigns of the last two years.
Let us first look at this affluent Canada. While we have much to be happy about there are still people in Canada who live at a level which is a disgrace. We should all be ashamed of conditions which we have allowed to develop and to continue, and which the minister has ignored completely in his budget speech. In fact the budget speech proposes that we permit the rich to get richer and the poor to get poorer by continuing the present and past tax inequities. He has thrown us the bone that, as soon as the royal commission makes its report, he will get down to looking at the situation; but I want to say that I have not much confidence in this minister or this government doing anything to rectify the inequities we have talked about so often in the past.
In 1961, the last year for which we have figures, 30 per cent of Canada's labour force earned so little money that they paid no income tax. Fifty five per cent of the taxpayers

earned less than $4,000 per year; 34 per cent of the taxpayers earned less than $3,000 a year and 14 per cent of those who paid taxes earned less than $2,000 per year. The top 25 per cent of taxpayers received almost 45 per cent of the total after tax income, while the bottom 25 per cent of taxpayers received less than 12 per cent of total after tax income. Despite these glaring and disgraceful discrepancies the minister proposes merely to continue to widen the tax exemptions and loopholes which have contributed to the inequities I have cited.
It is easy to get lost in statistics and figures, and because of this I should like to read a small section from an official report prepared for the Manitoba government, which I think has been received by all the members of this parliament. It shows graphically how badly some of the people in Canada are living. I refer to the original inhabitants of this country, the Indians of Manitoba. In this report, which is entitled "Manitoba, 1962 to 1975", and is a report of the committee on Manitoba's economic future, there is a section entitled "Role of native people in the north in industrial development". In part XI, section 3, pages 1 and 2, the following statements appear;
The native people of Canada in regions ranging from northern British Columbia to northern Quebec have not been integrated effectively into the social and economic fabric of the nation ...
The economic position and future status of native people in Manitoba presents three outstanding areas of concern. The level of social and economic integration of the group is very low and shows little improvement after almost 100 years of special administration. The levels of living and per capita earned income are little more than one tenth of those of the rest of the province...
The low level of social and economic integration tends to prevent any increase in per capita earned incomes. Low incomes and levels of living and increasing reliance on welfare tend to retard, or to prevent, improvement in social and economic integration.
I should just like the house and the minister to listen to these specific figures.
In 1981 per capita earned income of the group approximates only $155 per year, and without extensive rehabilitation and development measures, this low level of income can be expected to remain constant or even to decline during the next decade. Earned income is supplemented by family allowances, old age pensions, and various welfare payments from federal and provincial sources, which total slightly more than $100 per capita at present...
In the light of that kind of situation, Mr. Speaker, we have the self-satisfied speeches made by the minister and other members of the government. We talk movingly and feelingly about the plight of the people in underdeveloped countries of Asia, Africa and South America. I believe we could do much more to help them lift up their standards of living, but surely we should be moving quickly and

resolutely toward righting conditions here at home; and of this there is nothing at all for this in the budget presented by the minister.
I should like to contrast the minister's approach to the approval of the President of the United States. The United States is the richest, most affluent country in the world but, unlike the Minister of Finance, President Johnson has recognized that there are still large scale pockets of poverty in that country. At least 30 million Americans are poor. They lack the money, the education and the background to enable them to pull themselves up by their bootstraps. The President has declared a national war on poverty. He has called for a program which would cost $1 billion a year-organized and financed by the federal government-but administered through the state and municipal governments.
If this is necessary in the United States, how much more is it required in Canada? The President proposes that 100,000 young people be put to work in a national job corps on conservation and other projects, while also receiving education and training. There will be an organization called "Volunteers for America" which will supply helpers to work among Indians and migratory workers. Could we use such an organization in this country? Of course we could. Is one proposed by this government? Of course it is not. The President proposes to provide money to support families while mothers and fathers are training or retraining for jobs. There will be a work study program to provide parttime jobs for high school and college students.
We have made a beginning on this sort of program, but according to reports I have seen in Toronto newspapers a large percentage of the people who start on this kind of program in Canada stop before they are finished, because they cannot afford to stay away from any kind of job which would give them an income to keep their families while they are taking this job retraining.
The program which the President of the United States has proposed goes far beyond the now accepted idea in the United States or Canada that the needy are entitled to welfare to maintain them at a decent standard, or at least at a standard sufficiently high so that they will not starve. The program proposed in the United States will break the chain of relief and welfare which we have had in the past. It will provide the poor with new skills, new hope and a new environment. With such a program we could hope for an end to the poverty and degradation of so many of our people, but there is no evidence of that kind of approach on the part of the government, certainly not in the budget.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
I should like to deal with what I consider to be the most important defect of the budget, its almost complete failure to meet the educational and research needs of this country at a time when it is becoming obvious to the most dense that no country can progess in this age without a tremendously expanded effort in this field. Harold Wilson, leader of the labour party, has estimated that 97 per cent of all the scientists who have ever lived in the world are alive and working today. Yet in the past three years in Canada we have paid so little attention to the needs and desires of our most qualified and best trained people that over 120 professors and instructors in fields such as physics, biology, geology and chemistry left for the United States. In the same three years we permitted over 1,000 engineers to go to the United States, and we permitted over 1,000 physicians to leave for the United States.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that we should do anything to force these people to stay here but I do suggest that we ask ourselves why they went because the people who left were the youngest, the best, the most aggressive people that this country has produced. In a letter which I had recently from Dr. Hans Selye, world famous medical researcher at the University of Montreal, he told me that half of the people who qualify for their Ph.D. at his institute leave for the United States almost as soon as they finish. Why? Not because of salaries alone, but because of the research facilities, equipment and grants for research. Even the proposed increases in the estimates for this year are pitiful when compared with what is required.
I suggest that we look at what the situation is as set forth very clearly not by wild, idealistic, impractical people, which some in this house consider the members of this group to be, but rather as set forth in concrete proposals by authorized and most highly respected spokesmen for the universities and the research institutes of this country. In a brief to the Minister of Finance in December of 1963 the Canadian universities foundation made the following points:
-we suggested that the government of Canada establish a fund of $300 million for matching capital grants to universities and colleges. We wish to confirm the need and state that the urgency has now been compounded. We therefore urge that the operation of the fund be made retroactive to include projects undertaken after June 30, 1963.
And further:
We urge that the payment of university grants in 1964-65 the rate per capita of the population of the provinces be raised to $2.60, not by way of introducing any new principle but simply to keep this program from falling behind-
We reiterate our proposal that the Canada Council be assured of additional expendable funds

The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
amounting to at least $2 million per annum in order that it may provide sharply increased support for its program in the humanities and social sciences, including research collections in college and university libraries.
I ask, is there any sign in the budget or in the estimates that these carefully thought out and minimal requests have even been considered by the minister? The United States has almost 4,500,000 people in universities and institutions of higher education. A country like the Philippines, with a population of 23 million, had over 350,000 college students in 1960. A poor country like Puerto Rico, with two million people, had over
30,000	university students in 1960. Canada, with a population of 19 million and one of the highest standards of living, lags so far behind these countries that it is pathetic.
The Canada Council presented a brief to the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) on March 3, 1964. It pointed out that it has to provide support for all of the arts, humanities and social sciences and to finance the management of the university capital grant fund. What did the Canada Council tell the government in its brief? I should like to quote a couple of short sections from the brief:
The council is not now meeting the need, and will be increasingly unable to do so, unless its income can be sharply increased. We are consistently and repeatedly informed by our judges that out of the present number of applicants in most of our categories of scholarships we could justifiably select twice as many for awards as we are now able to do. If we were to undertake to meet the existing demands, an additional income of well over $500,000 a year would be needed. This is quite apart from the expected growth of the next few years.
And they say further:
In the 1962-63 report of the national research council the following figures are given: for scholarships, fellowships and associateships tenable in the universities, $1,980,000; and for grants in aid of research, $8,600,000, a total in round figures of $10,580,000. Over against this figure, the Canada Council can place not more than $1,200,000. We repeat that in the council's view this discrepancy is far greater than is justified by the needs of the country.
The council believes that the most practical way in which the government can give needed help is by making reasonable appropriations over a period of years. We therefore request the government to add during the present year a sum of $10 million to the endowment fund. We also request the government to consider the addition annually of $10 million for a further period of two years. When the endowment fund has been enlarged by $30 million, say in 1966, the developments of the three year period could be assessed, and whatever additional resources then demonstrated to be necessary could be agreed upon.
Was any real consideration given to these suggestions of the Canada Council? If there was you cannot find it in the budget or the estimates. The Ontario council of university faculty associations in a brief recently to


Premier Robarts has pointed out that university enrolment in that province will almost triple by 1971, and that the teaching staff will have to be quadrupled by 1971. They point out that Ontario universities have done their least impressive work in the fields of research, scholarships and graduate studies. A recent study of the larger Canadian university libraries showed there is not even one library which can be called first class in all of Ontario. If these are the facts in wealthy Ontario, how much worse is the situation in the rest of Canada?
What about scientific research, Mr. Speaker? Here the picture is little better. On December 5, 1963, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) received a letter from some of the most eminent medical research experts in Canada. I want to quote a couple of paragraphs from their submission. They say:
It has been clearly evident during the last decade that the support which is available for medical and biological research in Canada in the universities falls far short of that necessary to maintain the highest standards of scientific accomplishment.
And further:
-many of the most gifted young investigators, unable to find the means to carry out their research in Canada, have to find their opportunities for work elsewhere, mainly in the United States. This loss is not only felt in the organization of existing research groups but also in the education of future scientists, who are deprived of the contact with many of the best creative minds of Canada. It can be foreseen that the continuous process of depletion of the nation's talented personnel will have an adverse effect on the quality of research training and of teaching provided in the coming years when an expansion of the size of universities will be necessitated by the increased influx of students.
Have these serious questions been met by the government? In a speech made in Toronto, and reported in the Toronto Star of February 2, 1964, Dr. Hans Selye said that unless the Canadian government steps in with financial support, teams of researchers may be broken up and lost to Canada. He said it is possible that he might have to release as many as 40 of his 120 workers at the internationally famous institute of experimental medicine and surgery at Montreal. Dr. Stanley Hartroft, of the Toronto hospital for sick children, in the same story said the proposed increases for medical research are grossly inadequate and represent no actual increase to take up the projects dropped by the United States agencies.
In the new and vitally important field of nuclear medicine, there is also a vacuum. Senator Hubert Humphrey of Minnesota told the United States senate in 1960, that in the field of radiation research in life sciences, Canada was spending $1.25 million while the United States spent $63.5 million; only 71 persons were employed in this field in Canada,

while over 6,300 were employed in the United States; there were 82 projects being studied in Canada while over 2,000 were being studied in the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you compare the two countries, after adjusting for population you see that Canada is spending five times less money than the United States, is using nine times less the number of persons in this field and is working on two and a half times less projects. Can these scientists believe we really want them or need them in Canada? I am surprised, Mr. Speaker, that more of them have not left Canada than actually have left.
The Canadian association of physicists has for almost ten years been urging on Canadian governments, both Liberal and Conservative, the need for a program in the field of high energy physics to keep Canada abreast of the current work in this field. They prepared a report in July, 1963, which showed the trend in this field in other countries. This is a field which is basic to the development of modem physics. They urged the absolute necessity for the construction of a high energy particle accelerator if Canada is to offer to Canadian physicists the opportunity to do modern, challenging research.
There has been no response at all, at least no favourable response from this government. In their report, they point out that France, Britain and the United States are spending in this field from 30 cents to 60 cents per person per year. Countries such as Belgium, West Germany, Italy, Norway and Sweden are spending from 10 cents to 30 cents per person per year. Austria, Denmark and Holland are spending from 3 cents to 10 cents per person per year. Poor countries like Greece and Spain are spending from 1 cent to 3 cents per person per year. Wealthy, happy, stodgy, careless Canada is spending only one half cent per person per year. Is it any wonder that Canadian physicists leave? The wonder is that they have not gone faster.
If you look at the budget with that microscope which the lead speaker for the official opposition referred to the other night, you will find virtually nothing for these people in this budget or in the estimates which have been tabled. I think I have demonstrated conclusively that the bright, eager and hopeful approach apparently adopted by the Liberal party when in opposition has already been replaced by the stodgy, do-nothing, don't rock the boat approach so typical of the Liberals when they were in office. We would urge the government to remember its pledges to the Canadian people, to forget this budget and to move quickly to meet the real needs of the Canadian people which they
The Budget-Mr. Regan have for so long been ignoring, and which would make this a better, finer country for all the people.

I was greatly surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) because they were a harsh indictment of the budget. He has stated that this budget contained nothing new and that it was a very disappointing budget from his point of view. I could not disagree with him more. After a series of huge deficits in this country since 1956, a budget which chops one third off the deficit and

The Budget-Mr. Regan moves us toward a balanced budget, I consider to be a very significant achievement. A budget which provides family allowance increases for those of 16 and 17, about which I will say more in a moment-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will you be here next March?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We certainly will. A budget which is presented at a time when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is able to report that unemployment throughout the country has decreased substantially, at a time when prosperity and economic activities throughout the country are increasing significantly, a budget which specifically recognizes the need for education in this nation and provides a system of bank loans to our university students, is certainly a notable achievement. Mr. Speaker, I suggest this is a very significant budget and one that is in line with the responsibility of this government, and its aim to restore fiscal responsibility in the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You and Senator McCutcheon.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

He is richer. With reference to the extension of the family allowances to cover those of ages 16 and 17, I would point out that this is only one of the undertakings given in the Liberal election platform of last year, and that Liberal promises are being met one by one, to use Curzon's description, with the steady tramp of infantry across the field.
In so doing the pattern falls together, and I would point out that the paramount Liberal promise of them all was to restore fiscal responsibility to the nation, rather than continue with the handout, piecemeal policy of the previous government which inevitably led to record breaking deficits.
I listened carefully to the financial critic of the official opposition, and I hastily subscribe to his position as one of the deans of the opposition. I have referred to him without malice on many occasions as jovial George. Again he disclosed to us his fundamental weakness, which may very well be the source of his fundamental charm, and that is that in his criticisms he does not tell us the desirable policies omitted, nor the undesirable policies that were included.
Of course he chastised the Minister of Finance, as we would expect him to do. To do otherwise would be to make him derelict of his duty, and he has never been derelict of his duty. But listening to his remarks I came to the conclusion that the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) must consider this a darned good budget, otherwise as a former minister of finance he would have burned some midnight oil to try to tear it apart, which he obviously did not.


One wonders if he, like the majority of the people of Canada, feels once again Canada is on the road to stable government, something which was demonstrated by the accounting given to us last Monday night by the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Those of us from the smaller provinces become very concerned at some of the talk emanating from the provincial governments of Canada's two most populous provinces, to the effect that our constitution should be amended to strip the federal government of much of its taxing power, and hand these additional fields of taxation to the provinces.
Statements of this type, which have frequently been made by fuzzy-thinking empire builders of the Rene Levesque ilk, totally ignore the historical facts of Canada, and the existence within this confederation of provinces such as Nova Scotia, which bear the yoke of geographic disadvantage and the burden of a tariff structure that favours only central Canada. Do these powerful provin-cialists actually believe that Nova Scotians, Newfoundlanders and others would or could remain in confederation if the central government were stripped of its financial ability to carry out national policies that provide some recompense for the disadvantages I have already mentioned?
One of the things which has bothered me about the confederation dialogue that has been going on for the last two years or so is that it has been exclusively a dialogue between Ontario and Quebec. There are other provinces in Canada, Mr. Speaker.
