I would hasten to point out that with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick being partners in the original confederation we must remember that it was not at the time of confederation that Ontario and Quebec, that French and English, first joined together. They were committed to union some 26 years before, in 1841; but the leading citizens of those two states or provinces came to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island during the 1860's, at a time when their own financial difficulties had become so urgent, at a time when they could not get along, and at a time, in the words of Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, when it was felt that the addition of new partners would relieve the strain.
We did not come seeking confederation. We were the reluctant brides.

But we do become perturbed when some people from that province use this legitimate aim as a guise for obtaining unfair commercial advantage. I think you must remember that it is an integral part of confederation, if provinces at the geographical limits of the nation are to be a part of this nation and bear the tariff burdens that only help the central part of Canada, then if we are to suffer the disadvantages of our geographical position the federal government must be in a financial position to carry out equalization grants and other policies that keep us as an integral part of the country.
Before leaving this particular subject, Mr. Speaker, let me say that a perusal of the pre-confederation debates among the four original partners shows that there were guarantees given to the maritime provinces, for instance, on the question of winter navigation, and there is as much evidence that these guarantees were given to the maritime provinces as there is evidence that the French language had guarantees beyond the use of it in parliament and in the courts.

I am quite happy to say that, though the expressed words in the British North America Act do not go beyond that, it was the intention that the guarantees to the French language would go far beyond those words, and the contemporaneous utterances of a public statesman of the time showed also guarantees on winter navigation to Halifax and Saint John that were just as great as the guarantees to the French language.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unlike the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) I have not asked permission to leave, so I must continue my speech.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance recognizes the regional nature of unemployment as it exists today, and I noted from his remarks when presenting the budget that he thought that by far the highest unemployment exists in the Atlantic provinces. It is in the Atlantic region that unemployment continues to be a very severe problem and, unlike the previous administration, I do not think anyone on this side of the house has suggested that unemployment is not yet a problem. It has become a major regional problem and this government is determined that, even if the position has been improved in the Atlantic region during the past year, the improvement must continue until the problem is licked.
I would remark in passing that the Atlantic development board has moved during the past few months to expend usefully some of the $100 million which it has been given by this administration, and I think specific projects undertaken by that board will certainly result in great advantage. But the problem in the maritimes remains, as always, one of transportation. Until we have a realistic railroad policy based on the principle that the outlying areas of Canada should not be at a disadvantage, we cannot have real prosperity in that area.
The subamendment which was moved on behalf of the New Democratic party deplored the failure of the government to reduce defence expenditures. This approach is characteristic of the unrealistic, ivory tower attitude taken by that group toward the problems of defence and disarmament. It is well known that the most energetic and able minister of defence this house has seen in many years has already undertaken an extensive program of pruning the dead wood from defence expenditures with a consequential substantial saving in expenditures. The government has had drastically to revise the allocation of our defence expenditures because of failure to
1306	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Regan up-date plans in the years when this country was under the prime ministership of "the great procrastinator".
Apparently the subamendment expresses regret that defence expenditures have not been cut to a still greater degree. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), for whom I have the greatest respect, did not say one word in his remarks to indicate which specific defence expenditures should, in his opinion, be reduced, or precisely what aspect of the security of our nation should be neglected. I noticed also that his colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), speaking a few minutes ago did not even mention the subject of the subamendment. So he could not have been too much impressed by it. If an amendment of the type proposed by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands were to be introduced then, surely, it was the duty of members of his group to specify precisely where the suggested reductions should occur. At this very time, the participation of our nation in the peace keeping force in Cyprus is resulting in considerable unforeseen defence expenditure. But the hon. member who moved the subamendment appeared to praise our participation in the Cyprus affair and we must, therefore conclude that it is not in this area that he would economize.
I suggest we all remember that there are still abroad in this world strong forces which are hostile to the aims and aspirations of freedom loving democracies. What is more, these forces are working and watching for every opportunity to find the free nations with their guard lowered. Every hon. member of this house favours disarmament-but not unilateral disarmament, and not disarmament without safeguards as long as a threat to our security exists. Our nation must not shirk its responsibility to contribute, in accordance with its size and wealth, to the defence of the free world. If savings are to be made, subject to the provisos I have mentioned, then surely the minister, with the help of his advisers, is the person best able to determine where economies can safely be effected. The hon. gentleman's policies in the past few months have surely shown that he wishes to carry out whatever economies are possible, consistent with our obligations. Sometimes such economies are painful, but they are necessary. So, if members of the New Democratic party wish to see economies effected, let them tell us exactly what they would remove from our armed forces. As for me, I am confident that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) will, in his white paper, outline a program for the future which will provide that our men in the armed services have in [Mr. Regan.1

their hands at all times the best weapons and equipment which can be procured-all the material which is necessary to meet the modern scientific weapons possessed by any potential aggressor.
If I may say a further word on the subject of defence expenditures, I should like to deal with the question of pay for members of the armed forces. Shortly after coming to office last spring, the present government announced a pay increase for members of the armed services. While this increase was adequate to meet the needs of those serving in higher ranks, it provided only a very slim increase for the ordinary soldier, sailor and airman. My own experience in industrial relations has shown that the proper spread between the wages of higher and lower classifications can only be retained by alternating percentage and straight across the board increases, and I would urge the Minister of National Defence that when the remuneration of members of the armed forces is again reviewed particular attention be paid to the needs of the lower ranks, so that a high morale can be retained in our defence forces.
This is of the essence if our voluntary system is to continue to prove a success. I submit that in the post-war years this system has worked out much better than the draft system enforced in the United States. As a matter of fact there is every indication that the Americans are dissatisfied with their system at the present time, and that they are looking with some envy at ours. And the Canadian system will only continue to work as long as service in the armed forces provides an attractive career for our young men.
I should like now to say a word with regard to education, a subject on which I have already touched once or twice in passing. As I have mentioned, the measures to extend family allowances and provide for guaranteed loans for students are obviously part of a move to encourage students to continue their education at a time when the level of education is of great importance. In passing, let me say I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North as to the undesirability of so many people trained in Canada leaving to take up employment in the United States. I think steps should be taken in an effort to change this situation, if possible. However, if the policy of making loans to students is as successful as I think it will be, then it will aggravate another pressing problem, namely the need of various universities in Canada for additional physical facilities to enable them to accommodate all the students who are likely to seek enrolment. This is a need which will arise in an acute form in the future, and I submit that a great deal will have to be done

in this field. I might say that the province of Nova Scotia has always received an extremely raw deal in the matter of university capital grants made through the Canada Council. This is because the grants are made on the basis of the population of the various provinces; it has not been recognized that students come to our universities in Nova Scotia from all over the Atlantic provinces, and indeed from much of Upper Canada. The origin of the student population of our provincial universities must be recognized and considered as a factor in future, when direct grants are made.
Speaking of subsidies, we in Nova Scotia are subsidizing the business and professional life of Upper Canada by educating so many of its citizens in various professions and skills. It is true that of those who are educated in Nova Scotia, relatively few remain in the province because of the economic disadvantages we have suffered under confederation. I mention this in passing because I hope that in future attention will be given to the needs of the universities in Nova Scotia in particular.
I should like to say a word, too, on the subject of vocational assistance. The predecessors of this government were active in the field of educational and vocational assistance many years ago. I think that at the present time the change in the character of the skills and education needed in our citizens is such that a great deal of attention should be paid to this question of vocational assistance. I realize that this is largely a provincial field. Nevertheless I think I should be permitted to point out that in many instances the vocational and technical institutions of this nation are preparing our young men and women with training in relatively unimportant skills; they have still, I feel, to produce the skills which are needed in today's world, as is being done through similar programs in other nations.
I would give an example in my area, Mr. Speaker, the Halifax area. There we have a very fine electronics industry at E.M.I.-Cossor Electronics Limited. This plant finds they are unable to obtain in the Halifax area or in Nova Scotia, persons trained in electronics skills and they have to go again and again to England to find employees when they need them, and bring them over to Canada. We are extremely pleased to have these fine, new citizens in our area; but at the same time we think it unfortunate that there is not an expanded vocational training course in the area to cover these types of skills.
Mr. Speaker, all in all I think the word that would best describe the budget presented by the hon. Minister of Finance this week
The Budget-Mr. Paul
is that it is a sane budget; a budget that recognized the problems which face Canada; a budget which came less than a year after this government came into office but yet enabled the minister to come forth with a program that will result in the deficit of the previous year being decreased by one third, and which presented important, new programs to the people of Canada and got Canada squarely back on the road to stability and prosperity.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when, following the election of April 8, 1963, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was called upon to choose his cabinet, nobody was surprised to see the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) given that post because for almost two years his accession had been prepared. It was even said that he was the power behind the throne in economic matters w'ithin the Liberal party.
His first budget was awaited with anxiety and suspicion. Everyone recalls the evening of June 13, 1963, when the Minister of Finance, helped by a team of experts, went before the Canadian people to bring down his first budget. That evening, we were given a new economic theory which I shall call "Goraonism".
By putting this economic theory into practice, the Minister of Finance expected to balance his budget. As can be seen on page 999 of Hansard, this is what the minister said that evening.
But if this is to be justified and maintained it is important that we begin to put our national house in order: that we begin to move toward balancing our federal budget under conditions of high employment. We must take the first step in this direction now.
That is fine in theory, but the minister's statement is indicative of the qualified accountant who used his talents in the interests of his people but who, unfortunately, does not know much about practical administration.
Indeed, he was somewhat proud and arrogant when, on the night of June 13, he explained his theory to the house. However, what was excellent in theory was disastrous in actual practice, and the people of Canada were drugged into accepting new taxes.
However, the new drug proved to be a bit too strong for our country's economy.
Then, just as in the case of a seriously ill patient other experts' services were requested. Thus, we know that the Montreal stock exchange's president, Mr. Kierans, as well as other businessmen and brokers from Montreal met with the Minister of Finance. The minister was finally persuaded that the remedy he

The Budget-Mr. Paul
had advocated was too strong and that the dose had to be reduced. So we witnessed the reduction of the 11 per cent tax to 4 per cent; the second dose will be administered on the 1st of April next and the third, on January 1, 1965.
Even the minister was affected by that economic germ and for a while, we had fears for his political future. There were all kinds of rumours to the effect that he was falling out of the frying pan into the fire, that he should retire to other places, but the fact is that he remained in office.
This year, we saw the Minister of Finance come before the house without any experts to introduce exactly what? To introduce an empty and worthless budget. The minister is now affected by lazarism, which means he offered the Canadian people the crumbs of Lazarus referred to in the Gospel, and the remarks made by financial interests concerning the minister's budget are quite unanimous.
If I may, I should like to recall the opinion given by Mr. MacDonald, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Labour Congress, who said that the budget introduced last Monday was quite dull because it offered no new proposal to strengthen the Canadian economy. Mr. MacDonald also remarked, no doubt, the selfsatisfaction displayed by the minister when he introduced his budget because he firmly believed that his first budget was responsible for spurring on the economy of Canada, so much so that he believes himself responsible for the recovery of our economy which has taken place during the last few years, and which continued during 1963. But Mr. MacDonald did not agree with this opinion when he said:
The expansion we have known recently is due, for the most part, to fortuitous circumstances that have nothing to do with the measures taken by the government.
In an editorial published in La Presse of Montreal March 17, Mr. Vincent Prince reported that the budget was not a thriller.
In an editorial published in Sherbrooke La Tribune on March 18, reporter Pierre-Paul Blais wrote:
If a federal budget can help the Canadian economy and accelerate its growth rate, surely this will not be done by Mr. Gordon's new budget. He rather gives the impression that he intends to let the economy coast along on its own momentum in the hope that this will be enough to maintain prosperity at a satisfactory level and provide surplus income large enough to reduce the deficit by some $250 million.
I shall now continue my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by considering the budget from the Quebec point of view.
I listened with great attention to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) who tried to adjust the budget to the real needs of the

province of Nova Scotia. As I am a Quebec member, I think I should look at the budget from the Quebec angle.
First of all, I was disappointed to find that the budget does not say a thing about the claims of the premier of Quebec, the Hon. Jean Lesage, because they were not exclusively Quebec claims, but they expressed the needs of all provinces. Indeed, during the federal-provincial conference in 1963, the premier of Quebec made the following statement.
But this was not the main point of our requests. We also-and more particularly-wanted the federal government to evacuate to a greater degree the fields of individual income tax and corpora-ration profit tax and to surrender the estates tax. As a matter of fact, we suggested that the field be abandoned by the central government to the extent of 25 per cent in the case of the individual and corporation income taxes. We also asked the government to yield the whole field of estate taxation.
We may recall, the great service rendered by the Quebec premier and the spectacular action he took in the middle of the 1963 election, when he asked the people to support the Liberal party. Would the premier of Quebec make the same statement today, March 20, 1964, in favour of the Liberal team now at the helm in this country.
The federal budget does not say a single thing regarding the concessions which the government proposes to make to the provinces. We might well wonder about the reasons for which the hon. Minister of Finance submitted the budget at such an early date.
Does the government propose to go to the people in June, or did it resort to this trick in view of the conference of March 31, 1964, so as to be able to put forward some reasons and excuses for not following up the claims voiced during the last federal-provincial conference?
The provinces would then be placed before a fait accompli and at that time the Minister of Finance would be justified to say: "I understand the situation. We are willing to give it consideration, but unfortunately we have just tabled the budget". The provinces would still be deprived of their taxation rights which they need nevertheless to ensure a constant economic development.
There is no reason to be surprised because the federal government by itself does not create economic prosperity in the country; indeed, it is the prosperity of each Canadian province which gives economic prosperity to Canada.
The budget of the Minister of Finance does not say a word about the situation of the textile industry in the province of Quebec. Why? The province of Quebec has now the greatest number of unemployed, with the exception of the maritime provinces; 9.2 per

cent of our workers are now jobless, and what does the Minister of Finance do to help our textile industry which is peculiar to the province of Quebec? The minister of finance in the former government, Mr. Fleming, always had in every one of his budgets a provision concerning customs tariffs, in order to check the entry in this country of foreign textile products and help to safeguard to a higher degree this production which is peculiar to eastern Canada and especially to the province of Quebec.
Why did the Minister of Finance not make any provision in that respect? There are now 40 towns in the province of Quebec who need the textile industry for their living: Drummondville, Sherbrooke, St. Hyacinthe, Louiseville, Marieville, Montmorency and a number of others.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The riding of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope I will have time later on to refer to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). Why did the Minister of Finance not say a word about this matter? He could not do otherwise, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), whom I consider as a very efficient man, somewhat committed his government last August, by a statement he made on August 30, 1963, in order to facilitate the sale of wheat to red China. Please note that I am in favour of our wheat sales to red China, so much so that it was the Conservative party, through the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), which made every effort to promote the sale of our farm products to foreign countries.
This proves that the Conservative policy was excellent, from the point of view of international trade, but this trade was never carried on to the disadvantage of a particular class of people in Canada.
Why did the Minister of Trade and Commerce announce that imports of textiles from red China, which amounted to $3 or $4 million a year, would be increased to $7 million? Entries of textiles representing three million. To whose disadvantage? To the disadvantage of the wage earner who works in textile factories. Therefore, we should not be surprised if the Minister of Finance remained completely silent on that point.
I will point out to you that I do not speak about the remarkable silence of the budget as to the agricultural policy of the government, because we have at present a bicephalous department. There is no doubt about it. the minister for western Canada must be unaware of what the minister for eastern
20220-83i
The Budget-Mr. Paul Canada is doing and the dealings of the minister for western Canada must be unnoticed by the minister for eastern Canada.
There is only one thing left for us to do and that is to tell farmers of the province of Quebec: "Run away as fast as you can". When I say "run away", I am obviously not referring to the forestry minister, the hon. member for !les-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve).
No, there is a stubborn silence in regard to the agricultural policy of the country. And yet, heaven knows how farmers recall the wise policies implemented by the Conservative government to assist the dairy industry. It was decided to pay a subsidy on each pound of butter fat instead of paying 25 cents per hundred pounds of milk. The pattern of the subsidy was changed because it was alleged that farmers added too much water to the milk. Well, that is not the real reason. The real reason is that the Liberal government always promoted a farm policy favouring exclusively western Canada to the detriment of eastern agriculture.
As a matter of fact, only a few days prior to the overthrow of the Conservative government in February 1963, the former agriculture minister, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), presented a bill to promote further the farm economy of eastern Canada. Unfortunately, all that was thrown overboard when this government assumed power.
And what about joint programs? It is interesting to note the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in this connection. This is what he said last March 16 on joint programs:
We have no desire, however, to go on indefinitely levying taxes simply to pay for programs that are well established and well within provincial jurisdiction.
And now, what about the attitude of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who, a few days after he took office, decided that the government was not going to build the railroad between St. Anne des Monts and Gaspe? And I am also wondering what the hon. member from Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) is doing about making the necessary representations to the government in order to stimulate the economy in his area, which finds itself in a slump. Absolutely nothing. But the Minister of Transport said the government was going to contribute in a different way, that it was going to take part in joint programs, to develop country roads in that area.
The development of the rural economy, there you have the new policy of the Minister of Finance. But he does not give a hoot for the economy of the country as a whole. As a matter of fact, he relies on the tax

The Budget-Mr. Paul
cuts decreed by the United States government to activate the financial mechanism in such a way that the effects will be felt even in Canada and that, indirectly, the Canadian economy will benefit from that sound policy of the American administration.
But no tax reductions for this country. And yet, my Liberal friends, you had promised them. Here:
Tax reduction, a seven week tax holiday. Taxes cut by $400 million.
I ask the Minister of Finance to have a look at this, if he can see from that far away:
$400 million reduction.
He cannot have been that far away when the Liberal party prepared its economic and political propaganda in 1958.
A seven week tax holiday.
Taxes cut by 25 per cent for seven additional weeks.
No taxes to pay for three years in the case of newlyweds.
No, there is no tax imposed on newlyweds, but they are prevented from building new houses as a result of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
If you, Liberals, had promised us then that the government would be seven weeks without a minister of agriculture, you would have kept your promise.
Mr. Speaker, there is a matter which I cannot ignore, that of the crumbs or remnants which have fallen from the table of the Minister of Finance.
The $10 increase in family allowances-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is fine.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is fine, but finally you have understood that our party was in a position to submit effective solutions to the problems of our young students. But why did you vote against the motion of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) who, in February last, proposed a $10 monthly increase in family allowances? And yet, you made such a promise during the election campaign. But you would rather wait for the budget of the Minister of Finance to increase those allowances.
Other measures have also been taken to help university students. I congratulate the Minister of Finance. Thanks for those crumbs, but please give us more, give us a whole loaf.
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked by the government's attitude yesterday. In fact, when I asked the Prime Minister if he or his government had considered the constitutional aspect of grants to students, the Prime Minister replied overbearingly: We never do anything which would infringe upon the rights of the provinces.

And yet, who introduced legislation designed to help municipalities at the expense of provincial autonomy?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did he consult the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the hon. member for Halifax is no longer here, because I would have called his attention to section 93 of the British North America Act which reads as follows:
In and for each province, the legislaure may exclusively make laws in relation to education.
Under this section, therefore, the provinces are given exclusive jurisdiction with regard to education. In addition, the jurisprudence of the supreme court and of the privy council has been consistently along the same lines as to the meaning of the word education.
The scope of section 93 was definite for the province of Quebec during the conferences held prior to the passage of the confederation act. The incorporation of section 93 into the confederation act was demanded and granted, because it was essential to the safeguard of the French language, culture and personality. It was also essential to the survival of French Canadians, because in 1867 Quebec was the only French speaking province among the four provinces of confederation. Today, Quebec is still the only French speaking province. It is therefore more than ever necessary that it should keep complete control in the field of education. It is through its education system that the French personality blossomed out, or at least survived, in Canada, and French Canadians wish to preserve their personality and to develop it in the interests of the whole country. French Canadians hope, wish and want to make their culture available to the Canadian people, and not to the separatists of the province of Quebec.
The government might reply that by passing legislation to grant scholarships to students, it is not interfering with education. One cannot do directly what one is forbidden to do indirectly.
A good Liberal told me lately that it was a moral obligation for the federal government to help the young people to further their studies, to help them, by all possible means, to get an education, so that they would have a first class position tomorrow in our society.
In constitutional law, where do we find that moral obligation? The federal government's moral obligation, I think, is to transfer more to the provinces, to grant them better taxation rights so that they can meet today's needs in the field of education. That is one way the government would be able to assist the provinces, and not by granting scholarships because they have been censured by everybody.

Some might say: If the government grants unconditional loans what have you got to fear?
We have to consider the future and create no precedent which would open the door to abuses. We have no right to mortgage the future of our young people. As long as our country is governed by one of the big parties, there will be no danger that French Canadians lose their identity, their past and their culture. But should one day socialists, such as we have in the left corner of this house, or right-wing extremists, such as we have in the left corner of this house, come to power, then there would be cause for concern.
Then the future and French culture would be in danger in Canada because the jurisdiction is well established: let Quebec look after education, let the provinces look after education. Besides, that is the present policy of the Quebec government-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Separatism.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member for Villeneuve mention separatism. But when you talk of separatism, do so in the English provinces as well as in the province of Quebec, and not only in Quebec, trying to pit the provinces one against the other. When one has principles, one puts them into practice, in English Canada just as well as in French Canada, and vice versa. Not only one way in one province and another way in another province.
You ate pork and beans in St. Angele de Prevost last Saturday night, come and talk about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to talk to the Chair?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would rather give you food for thought. I leave culinary matters to the hon. member for Villeneuve.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin), parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, seems to agree with the premier of Quebec, for he said last night: I will discuss this matter of loans to students at the next federal-provincial conference because it is another case of federal interference in the field of education.
We remember how strenuously the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska objected to the present policy of the Liberal government. We remember also how various university associations of the province of Quebec protested against this intrusion contemplated by the federal government.
What is co-operative federalism leading to? It will lead to centralization, if we do not check its advance. I wonder what will be the
The Budget-Mr. Marcoux attitude of my Quebec colleagues when this question is discussed. They had taken a definite position with regard to nuclear arms; everyone kept remarkably silent when this question came before us.
Let us hope that there will be fortunate exceptions. For instance, one hon. member had the courage to blame his party leader during an election campaign.
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to deal with other matters; unfortunately, I have only two minutes left. We shall be called at a quarter to five to vote on a motion introduced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron).
I would have liked to say something about the C.B.C. But my time is too short. It would have been interesting to know why the president of the C.B.C. received a $20,000 pay boost. No answer was given to a question to that effect put on the order paper by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard).
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will be possible for the Conservative party to support the subamendment moved by the New Democratic party.
As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) said a moment ago, we cannot adopt this proposal for it does not clarify in any way the areas where the federal government will have to reduce the expenses of the Department of National Defence. Personally, I do not believe that the reduction in these expenses represents the necessary reason or incentive that would give an impetus to this country's economy. That is the reason why the Conservative party will vote against this subamendment.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) introduced this year a limp and unspirited budget. I hope he will take into consideration the needs of the provinces and that on March 31 next, he shall, with his usual smile, firmly resolve to think about them and to find economic incentives without relying only upon the American economic development.
We may be right in hoping that the Canadian economy will keep on improving, not on account of the legislative measures taken after the introduction of the budget by the Minister of Finance but chiefly because the Conservative party had provided for certain economic measures that would permit to stimulate and to develop this country's economy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere (Mr. Paul) has not used his great oratorical talent to convince the Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Marcoux Finance last year of introducing a budget where we could-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were not there because a budget was tabled in April 1962.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The people had been requesting a budget lor a long time but no one could present one. Mr. Speaker, I submit that the situation is hardly better this year than last year when no budget was presented since the present budget contains very few new provisions and hardly anything which will satisfy the Canadian people.
The only people who will get certain benefits are the students and those advantages are far from being as great as some would have us believe.
For instance, everybody knows that parents are entitled to a $350 tax deduction for children who get family allowances. If you add to that the $10 a month family allowance, you get an additional amount of $120 for a grand total of $470 for deduction purposes. On the other hand, in the case of children who are not entitled to family allowances, parents are allowed to deduct $550 a year from their income tax.
Obviously, in this case, the amount of $120 for each child will be an additional amount which he can use. But, if we use the accountants' language, with assets and liabilities, we soon realize that, at the end of the year, instead of deducting $550 for each dependant child going to school, the family head will be able to deduct a maximum of $470. Everything taken into account, I would not say that this aspect of the budget is so beneficial to the father of a family who maintains children at school, in spite of the fact that the bill seems very interesting for students of 16 and 17 years of age, if this part of the budget is applied.
With reference to part-time students, 1 imagine that several may be helped in this way, being able to deduct their total school expenditures from their income.
But, in addition, I feel there is nothing in the budget indicating that the Canadian people will get any relief from taxation.
And now, in spite of heavy pressure on the part of manufacturers in general and associations of contractors, requesting the government to abolish the tax on building materials, or at least not to increase it beyond 4 per cent, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) refused to listen to any of them, although they are, after all, experts in their field, since the construction industry is their means of livelihood and since they are in a position to relieve unemployment.
In that field, the Minister of Finance has not seen fit to follow their advice. He has


rather followed the advice of his party, and maybe that of his own officials, so that the tax will gradually reach 11 per cent. That measure will surely have a harmful effect on the building rate in Canada and also on the number of unemployed, because when building is at a low level, unemployment is at a high level.
We would also have liked the government to define its policy with regard to receipts for charitable donations. For several years now, it has been said that this matter is creating enormous problems for the Minister of National Revenue and that a clear policy should be defined in that connection.
In my opinion, it is unfortunate that the Minister of Finance has not seen fit to define the government position concerning receipts for charitable donations. The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) has already provided a solution which would be fair, in my opinion, to most Canadians, to those of the province of Quebec as well as those of any other province. The minister has not paid any attention to it. I hope that, in the near future, that matter will be settled once and for all, because it embarrasses the clergy as well as those who want such receipts. It embarrasses also the hon. members who try to stand up for them before the officials of the Department of National Revenue who seem to understand nothing at all and believe that everybody is dishonest, except themselves.
I believe it is time for the government to determine a specific policy about this and for the policy of the Department of National Revenue to be, once and for all, well understood.
We would have liked also that a municipal development bank be established in order to allow municipalities to create new jobs, not small jobs such as those offered by the winter works program, or other small jobs that you can get under the Centennial of Canadian Confederation Act. We would have liked that such a bank be established in order to allow municipalities to develop and solve the regional and local unemployment problem, since the Minister of Finance says that the solution to unemployment is rather a regional problem.
I think such a bank would be the only way to assist our municipalities to get out of our present unemployment situations.
Since the Minister of Finance is prepared to permit the establishment of the Western Bank-he also seems prepared to authorize the establishment of the British-Columbia Bank-I think he should also be prepared to allow the establishment of a municipal development bank which would, at long last,

enable public bodies to use capital made available to them by the Canadian government.
Reference was also made to deficits. They are discussed all the time, and so is the public debt, the national debt. I do not want to labour the point, but I would remind the minister once more that in 1962-63, according to Canada Public Accounts, volume I, the nation paid in interests only on the public debt the amount of $881,598,898, while the defiicit came to $691,632,927. The deficit was smaller than the amount we paid in debt interests only.
If the solution we offer is not to be accepted another should be worked out because it is absolutely impossible to go on this way.
Once again, I do not wish to discuss the net national debt or the gross national debt, because investments and capitalized assets must be taken into account.
But considering only the amount required to pay interest on the debt and on the deficit, we find that there is a lag, indicating the folly of the system and that we cannot indefinitely keep on with this tempo; despite the fact that we wish to protect private enterprise, it is impossible to carry on this policy as we are doing now.
I am asking all those who deem themselves competent and able to resolve this problem- I can see many accountants and many economists on the other side of the house-to try to find a way that would enable us to get out of an economic position that has become really disadvantageous and which, instead of allowing us to become masters in our own house, in spite of all the fine speeches we constantly hear in this regard, is leading us more and more towards "americanization" instead of directing us towards total independence with respect to the United States.
In this regard, I should like to say a few words concerning the report of the O'Leary commission. The Conservatives will probably try to accuse the Liberals of not having carried out the recommendations of that commission. I will call to their attention that, as early as last year, a similar bill was to be presented.
By the way, I should like to quote a few newspapers, a few editorials which indicate that, for reasons unknown to us-I should say for reasons which we suspect too well, alas-the government did not deem it advisable to take into consideration the recommendations of the O'Leary commission. I should like to quote an editorial published last month in the Toronto daily Star where it is said that, at this time, it is not too late. So I speak now, for before long it will be too late. The article says:
The Budget-Mr. Marcoux

Fortunately the die has not yet been cast; the legislation has not yet been brought down. There is still time for the government to revise its bill to incorporate the full recommendations of the O'Leary commission, with no exceptions for Time, Reader's Digest or anyone else. This is a chance for Mr. Pearson and his colleagues to show that they have the strength to resist American pressure.

I should like to quote another editorial of the same newspaper, dated February 24: [Text]
Far from correcting the situation, the proposed legislation would give Time and Reader's Digest the status of Canadian publications. It would even protect them against competition from any other foreign magazine which might in future try to imitate their methods.

This is very serious, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that this government will begin to take those recommendations into account.
May I quote another article from the Toronto daily Star dated March 17:
The Canadian people have a right to insist that Time and Reader's Digest exemptions be wiped out before the legislation is passed.

I have here an article from the Globe and Mail which does not deal with the O'Leary commission, but quotes an actress from Sweden, Miss Greta Thyssen, as saying on her arrival in a Toronto hotel, after looking at the newspaper stand:
"You don't have any magazines of your own here?" she asked. "Such a rich country-why is everything American?"

Such is the impression of foreigners when they arrive in our country and look at newspaper stands.
May I quote another article from the Montreal Star dated March 19:

It it was china or tinware, if it was boots and shoes, if it was shirtwaists or any other form of textiles, the government would have moved in, horse, foot and artillery, to stop the imports. But these two magazines import into this country their whole editorial content, collected at a cost greatly exceeding the budget available to any Canadian magazine, and use it as the bait to attract advertising which might otherwise be available to a genuine Canadian magazine.
And later on the article goes on:
What is of particular interest to Montreal is that these perversions are both "produced" here.

The Budget-Mr. Marcoux
Time operates an editorial office in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, represented in parliament by the Liberal, Mr. John Turner. It is printed in the town of Mount Royal, represented in parliament by Mr. Alan Macnaughton, also a Liberal. Reader's Digest is "produced" in a leased building in the riding of St. Antoine-Westmount, which is represented by the Liberal Minister of Industry, Mr. C. M. Drury.

Here, I do not wish to accuse the Liberal party, because last year, under a Conservative administration, the introduction of a similar bill was contemplated.
I think that this year, we should go hand in hand as we did on the Maritime Union Trustees Act, because we are concerned with the protection of a Canadian industry. All parties should join together to recognize that Time and Reader's Digest are a nuisance for Canadian publications.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) who likes to specify that members he refers to are not in their seat-I shall tell him that he is not in his seat-discussed a while ago the matter of a Gaspe peninsula railway between St. Anne des Monts and Gaspe. I should like to point out on that matter that the railway was to go from Matane to St. Anne des Monts.
I have long been interested in that matter of a railway for the Gaspe peninsula because I am a lover of that region. I have been going there every year for a number of years and last year I was disgusted when I witnessed the type of election patronage carried on by the Conservatives. At the time I asked the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), a question. That question, which was put on the order paper on December 3, 1962 under number 1,007, was as follows:
What progress has been made in the construction of the railway line between Matane and St. Anne des Monts, and has section 6 of the enabling act been complied with?
Let us recall that section 6 provided that the minister of transport must bring a report before parliament within the first 30 days of the session before the date of completion set or forecast in section 1. At that time, no report had been made and here is what Mr. McBain, then parliamentary secretary to the minister of transport, replied:
(e) The Canadian National Railways are making a detailed survey but the report on that survey has not been received yet.
That was on December 3, 1962, and the bill had received royal assent on March 23, 1962.
A report for the year 1962 will be submitted to parliament early in the new year.
[Mr. Marcoux.1

Now, Mr. Speaker, we know that an order in council was passed on April 5, 1962, under P.C. No. 1962-481 and that another one was passed on May 2, 1962, under P.C. No. 1962656.
The latter provided the C.N.R. with an amount of $100,000 to start on the project and to be used during the period between April 16 and June 30, 1962.
We have a report from Mr. Gordon, the president of the C.N.R., dated June 18, 1962, no, that is the elections took place on June 18, and it is very important to insist on that, for before the elections, orders in council were passed, and they tried to buy a good number of votes by suggesting that the people living in the Gaspe peninsula would get a railway.
In May 1962, or June 1962, it is somewhat difficult to tell, the Canadian National Railways handed back to the crown an amount of $30,000, alleging that an amount of $70,000 sufficed to pay the cost of engineering works necessary for the preparation of estimates.
Mr. Speaker, the former prime minister stated at the time, as reported in the Quebec newspaper Le Soleil, and I quote:
You shall have your railway, said the Prime Minister before the crowd attending the meeting last night.
The railway was never built because it was not profitable, but especially because the Conservative party never intended to build it, despite the passing of an act. Strangely enough, previously, very few people, if any member of the Conservative party, even the former prime minister, knew that the line connecting Mont Joli and Matane was the property of the Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway Company and did not belong to the Canadian National Railways. The railway was the property of the abovementioned company, and this company demanded, for the use of its tracks, the sum of $110,000 per annum. However, all those details were learned afterwards, which makes it possible to tell the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Dela-naudiere that his party never intended to help this area much more than the Liberal party.
I do not wish to elaborate, since I know the hon. member for Levis has requested that some 20 minutes be left for him.
And speaking of Gaspe, it reminds me of the Trans-Gaspe Television Company which, for the past five years or so, has been trying to obtain a private station to serve the Gaspe area, which, in some districts, has no television service yet. Some people objected to that television station, and an indescribable pressure was brought to bear. I do not want

to describe what happened at this time, but perhaps the day will come when I can deal with it more fully.
After having heard the television company's request, the board of broadcast governors gave a negative answer pretexting some technical matter. Yet, when the directors of the company succeeded in settling the technical problem, they approached the B.B.G. once more and their request met with a refusal. Whereas, at the start, the request had been refused on technical grounds, it now was rejected for some financial reason.
Now, the financial problem having also been settled to everybody's satisfaction, the operators again approached the board of broadcast governors and, once again, the governors refused them a permit, while allowing two other television stations to extend their services, suggesting that, at some places, they establish satellite stations, which would not pay their way and are giving no results whatsoever, because those private companies had to limit their service to the areas allotted to them.
It was also pointed out that the C.B.C. should have priority over private stations when extending its network.
Well, let the C.B.C. come to an understanding with the operators of that station in order to be in a position to provide a service to those people who now are not getting any.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere and many others seem to think of the Gaspe peninsula as a neglected area. That is true. But when we say that it is neglected, even as far as television is concerned, I maintain that the government has got to do something. If the members of the board of broadcast governors refuse to co-operate and to change their decisions, well, let the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) be compelled to grant a licence, in spite of the decision of the board of broadcast governors.
There are some who might claim that the project is not economically sound. I have looked into that side of the question. True, I am no expert, but I did study the matter, and even the operators of the company that wanted to build the station are ready to finance the project. That goes to show that the area is recognized as economically sound and that the company would be able to serve its people. The operators have the means to do it. There is absolutely no reason why they should be prevented from building a television station to provide a service that the people in the Gaspe peninsula have a right to expect, for they are human beings just like any other citizens from any other area in this country.
The Budget-Mr. Guay
Mr. Speaker, I want to be brief in order to comply with the wishes of the hon. member for Levis. However, there are a few comments I wanted to make about the Beauport shore line. We have there a problem which the Minister of Transport, in co-operation with the national harbours board, should make up his mind to settle once and for all, because it has been under consideration for eight years. Besides, some individuals paid as much as $18,000 for land surveying, but unfortunately, the problem was submitted to the only legal adviser of the national harbours board and that adviser did not have time yet to make a decision. In my opinion, this situation is rather discouraging for the owners of properties on the shore of the Quebec harbour and along the St. Lawrence river.
Mr. Speaker, I will restrict myself to these remarks for the time being, but I shall have the opportunity to deal with this matter later on.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank especially the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) who was kind enough to give me a few minutes of his time to enable me to deliver my first speech in the house.
I should like to deal briefly today with some objectives of the budget introduced recently, and also with some results which can be expected.
Mr. Speaker, on taking part in this debate after several members on this side of the house, I wish to pay tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and reiterate our entire confidence in him.
In this budget, there is one thing which especially holds my attention; it is that the government has devoted an important part of the budget to students. Indeed, I am especially interested in the problems of students, because it was somewhat my own case about two years ago.
I am very grateful to the government for having increased the tax exemption from $300 to $470, for having allowed the deduction of the part-time students' school fees and especially for the $10 family allowance to students 16 and 17 years of age. In addition, I would be very pleased to see the establishment of an interest free loan system guaranteed by the government without any tax increase.
I am also proud to note that the government did not forget private businesses by extending our tax exemptions till 1967. As the Minister of Finance pointed out, the economy of the country has improved and I will add that it is especially in good hands. Unemployment has not been as low for years. The

The Budget-Mr. Guay prospects for 1964 seem, therefore, bright and all Canadians have regained confidence in the future.
Of course, hon. members opposite criticized the budget, as they have the right to do, but if they had analysed as closely their own budgets from 1957 to 1963, if they had really taken the trouble, on the occasion of every one of those budgets, to pass if only one really important piece of legislation to promote the economy and check unemployment, the situation on April 8, 1963, would not have been what it was. Fortunately, our government took the situation in hand. The measures taken in the first budget introduced by the Minister of Finance proved to be the best and that he was right.
That is why he still enjoys my confidence and I endorse his views. Like all previous speakers, I should like to state my personal opinion concerning the current problems of bilingualism and biculturalism.
Governments must act, first of all in order to repatriate our constitution and then to amend it, so that it might be better adapted to our rights and aspirations in this 20th century, and this goes for English Canadians, French Canadians and Canadians of other ethnic origin. I should like very much that French Canadians with equal qualifications might have the right to hope for high positions, executive posts in all departments. That way, in all departments, the French Canadian voice would be better heard, better understood and better respected. In fact, how many departments and crown corporation do not have enough French speaking officials? Therefore, it is my contention that this problem will be settled to everyone's satisfaction at government level. In that respect, it is satisfying to note a significant improvement in the situation through government's efforts and officials' co-operation.
Hear, hear.
Except three English speaking deputy ministers in key departments.
I hope the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm will let me finish my speech. However, I will not follow his example; should he ask me a question, I will answer it.
Will the hon. member allow a question?

Yes, when I have finished my speech.
The present government has done a lot but we will have to do even more otherwise we run the risk of failing, of never finding a solution to the problem. Everybody is ready, English Canadians, French Canadians, in

short, Canadians. Let us do something for it is high time we did. We want a true solution, otherwise separatism, which I would call extreme nationalism, and which is rearing its head in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces, will gain impetus and disaster might become unavoidable.
It is often said that separatism is unthinkable but the longer we shall wait to settle the problem, the more we will be reminded of it. We cannot indulge in the luxury of ignoring separatism, but we cannot cure the evil by a mere poultice, because we will have to start all over again in 15 or 20 years from now. We must find a proper solution and there is only one. I trust that the present government has in co-operative federalism a formula better than any other formula ever introduced before. Dialogue has started and must be carried on. Thus, our Prime Minister and the premiers of the ten provinces will find this solution and the appropriate medicine will be administered by a specialist who was able to diagnose the disease and to understand the aspirations of both ethnic groups, having in mind this old saying that the most bitter medicine is often the best. We must not be soft spoken, but firm and wise.
Of course, there is no question of accepting only compromises; we must be firm, but we must remember that the other party has problems also. The province of Quebec does not seek only to obtain concessions; it will actively co-operate in the solution of all the problems, not only of its own.
In my opinion, the Prime Minister has found the right formula, that of a dialogue carried on at federal-provincial conferences and which, in a single year, has given more than all the fine speeches made and all the sanctimonious principles voiced by all the parties. Let us put an end to empty speeches. We must now take concrete action. As I say, we must act because the situation is urgent. We have discovered the first symptoms, so let us not wait until the cancer has become generalized. Thus, we will have worked towards a common goal and, in 1967, we will all be happy citizens of a strong and united country which will have a new and dynamic constitution; we will celebrate the centennial of confederation and the first day of our rejuvenation in the best interest of all and of national unity. Because, in unity alone, we will be able to make of our Canada one of the chief powers in the world before the end of the centutry. Quebec's independence will never be profitable in any respect to herself or to the rest of Canada. We French Canadians have rights and we intend to have them respected, but, on the other hand, we know that others have equal rights and we intend to respect them.

It does not mean melting the two races, the two cultures, but rather uniting them in order that they may understand and respect each other better, and to define my thought more clearly, may I quote Mr. Marcel Faribault who said recently:
Culture may also describe the social characters of a people, of which it is a jealously guarded secret treasure: a treasure, because it belongs to that people alone; a secret, because it always includes slight faults and, at last, a jealously guarded object, because it could not be fully experienced or embraced other than by marriage or by being adopted in the family.
As far as Quebec was concerned, the problem appeared simple enough, and since it is an indubitable fact that there are in Canada two great cultural and linguistic currents, should there not be a degree of reciprocity between them, based on mutual respect, social exchanges and means of communication? Relations should, therefore, constitutionally, socially, politically and economically, stem from the establishment of definite institutions. However, the two extremist factions contest these premises: at one end are those who contend that all this is refinement which will fade away in the face of national unity; at the other, those who say that not only two but several cultures are in conflict. The first objection, from the point of view of unity, is obviously the result of confusing political unity with cultural unity: it ignores the fact that our federal form of government, contrary to its American counterpart, is not primarily based on sectional considerations, but on the two cultures which at that time divided nearly equally the majority of the population. Five and a half million Canadians, or 30 per cent of the population, are a constant reminder, a constant assertion, of this duality, since they relentlessly protested for the past 94 years against all customary amendments to the provisions of the pact of 1867 and, today, they are practically unanimously requesting a revision of the constitution. The dissidents, they are few and far apart, have simply given up hope of obtaining the revision and that is why they favour independence, just like all Irredentists.
Mr. Speaker, as a member from a constituency whose main industry is the shipbuilding, I am naturally most interested in that industry.
There is great concern in the shipbuilding industry at the present time, especially since the program for the building of frigates has been cancelled and Great Britain has been awarded a contract, following previous commitments of the former government, to build three submarines.
In my opinion, it is urgent to solve this problem by establishing a merchant marine.
20220-84J
The Budget-Mr. Guay This would create employment not only in shipyards but also for seafarers. Otherwise we might see the closing of our shipyards and an alarming increase of unemployment in all areas where they are located. The shipbuilding industry instead of becoming one of the chief industries of our country would be done away with and this would be disastrous for all of us.
In my constituency and also in nearby ridings it is customary to say that when shipyards are doing well, everything is fine. For us, when the shipyards are running smoothly the whole economy of the area benefits, and vice versa.
I have already made several representations to certain ministers in order to obtain employment for the workers of my constituency; they thought I was stubborn, but I wish to let them know that I will persist and that next time, I will even be more stubborn. I shall renew my efforts, because I am only demanding our fair share of work with no intention of depriving the others of anything.
The people of my riding are hard working, proud and quite determined. And who could blame them? That is why I wish to make it clear that we too are strongly against the vile political haggling of government favours that goes on too often, unfortunately. We are not asking for more in order to get less. As responsible citizens well aware of the huge needs of the whole country, we are only asking for what we are entitled to.
Levis is an important area of Canada, and our great province is an integral part of Canada. Quebec has largely contributed in the past to the development of the country and I have the firm conviction that its contribution will be much greater in the future.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who is well aware of the situation, is kindly asked to give it a special consideration and to take the necessary steps to ensure the survival of that important industrial centre on the south shore.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget the protests voiced by several labour unions with regard to the construction, in Japan, of 18 freighters, at the cost of $1 billion, on behalf of Canadian Javelin Company, for transportation of iron ore of our country, outside our boundaries. It becomes obvious that we must protect our shipyards. Time has come for us, now more than ever, to build our own merchant marine.
At this point, I should like to quote from bulletin No. 5 of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, but time does not permit it.

Division
In an average year, more than 141,000 ships, ocean-going or coasting vessels, load and unload in Canadian harbours, some 102 million tons of goods from all the countries in the world. If Canada wants to get its share of this important industry, there is no doubt that it needs its own merchant marine and modern and active shipyards.
There is reason to believe that Canada intends to devote more attention and efforts to the study of our coastal waters, including the Arctic. On both sides of the Atlantic, governments are beginning to realize the great resources to be derived from the waters covering their country's continental shelf. Should they lag behind in the race towards full development of the wealth of the sea, nations will put the coming generations under a heavy handicap.
That is why, rather than just for strategic or military reasons, the Soviet union and the western countries are studying the matter and taking steps to develop the resources of the sea. Without an ocean-going merchant marine and any harbour facilities, even a country like Canada, with its 20,000 miles of coast line, can actually miss the boat.
A maritime nation without ocean-going ships, without modern harbours and well-equipped shipyards is a paradox we cannot afford. That is why, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the report made by the royal commission on coastal trade published in 1957, I shall submit to the government a few proposals which I consider urgent.
1.	That the jurisdiction over coastal trade be extended up to the strait of Belle Isle, Newfoundland being a Canadian province.
2.	That ships be built and repaired in Canada, be registered in Canada and have their home ports in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: NOTICE TO PARLIAMENT OF EXTENSIONS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-8, to amend the Broadcasting Act (disclosure of C.B.C. service extension programs, cost, and estimates for five years).
He said: This is a very narrow bill, but before I launch into the reasons for it I think it is always fair, when you are speaking of the C.B.C. to make some general remarks by way of introduction. This is partly because this is a famous Canadian institution, partly because it is notorious and partly because its reputation, to say the least, is equivocal.
I should like to make the point immediately that this bill has the approval of my colleagues and reflects our party's attitude toward this particular segment of the C.B.C. In this party we happen to be, like other parties in the house, great proponents of the C.B.C. but at the same time some of us are very critical of the C.B.C. In essence, this bill represents a criticism of the way the C.B.C. has gone about extending its services in the last decade or so, particularly since television has become important. It is an attempt to put an onus upon the C.B.C. to be much more clear and direct in its policy with regard to the extension of services.
Before I get into that, Mr. Speaker, I think it is well to remember that in the area of broadcasting and a national broadcasting
Broadcasting Act
policy, you not only have a number of agencies involved in actual broadcasting, such as public broacasters and private broadcasters, but there are other agencies including the Department of Transport through the Radio Act licensing, organizations such as the community antennae organizations and also the board of broadcast governors. There is also the fact that the cabinet or government at any time has a general responsibility to have a broadcasting policy for the country that enables both the country and parliament, as well as members of parliament, to see just what is intended.
It has been my conviction for a number of years that the whole broadcasting policy of this country has tended to be fudged and blurred. We had a typical example yesterday when the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamon-tagne) brought into this house, at long last three years after the question was first raised, a statement concerning the policy, intentions and beliefs of the board of broadcast governors with relation to community antenna television. This is just an indicator of the confusion. One of the reasons that we have a problem with community antenna television in this country at the moment is that in the past the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation moved so slowly, without making any projections of how it was going to extend services in this country. I know personally of at least six places in this country that have community antenna television systems for which people are paying individually as much as $125 for installation and $5 per month in charges. This would never have been necessary if the C.B.C. had risen to its responsibilities to cover the country.
In its last annual report concerning television the C.B.C. maintains it covers 92 per cent of the country. One of the reasons they can make this statement is that a great many Canadians are paying through the nose for their hook-up with community antenna television service. There is still 8 per cent of the country that requires to be served by this Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
One of the effects of this bill, as anyone can see if he looks at the explanatory note, is a minor change to section 36 of the Broadcasting Act. The corporation would be required to append to its report particulars of each extension to the national broadcasting service within Canada that was undertaken or completed during that financial year, the cost thereof, as well as particulars of each such extension the corporation proposes to undertake or complete during the five financial years next ensuing, and the estimated cost thereof.
To members of the house who may be critical of this bill, I would say you can divide
HOUSE OF COXviMONS
Broadcasting Act
it up into two parts. First of all, if any hon. members look at the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, they will quickly see that the president is not reticent at all about setting forth any extensions of service. However this is always done within the text. There is no clear picture, beyond just the individual extension such as, for example, an extension to Dryden, Sioux Lookout and Kenora or the extension up into Thompson lake area a few years ago. We cannot see this very clearly.
Hon. members are more likely to question requirements projected for five years ahead. I should like to suggest to you that the C.B.C. itself, and many people interested in broadcasting, have been asking for a five year projection. As a matter of fact, in our broadcasting committee in 1961, this was perhaps the main thing that Mr. Ouimet brought before us at that time. At one time during the hearing, he gave an outline of the projections. It can be found at page 803 of the proceedings of the broadcasting committee in 1960-61. I am reading from a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation forecast of operating costs in revenue years 1962-63 to 1966-67. Anyone who will take the trouble to compare this forecast with what has actually transpired in the last two years will find that, in terms of parliamentary grants, the C.B.C. has been fairly accurate. The grants have been maybe $2 or $3 million under the estimates. What happened from 1960 onward is that the C.B.C. did not forecast the increase which took place in its commercial revenues. Nevertheless, this forecast indicated that the C.B.C. could really make a good projection.
If anyone cares to look at page 804 he will find in appendix B a five year projection of proposed expansion from 1961-62 through 1965-66 included in one of the items as improvement in coverage. The figures are as follows:	in 1961,	$1,907,000; in 1962-63
$2,717,000; in 1963-64, $2,078,000, and so on. It goes right through to the end of 1966, and the total for the five year period is $9,925,000. I want to point out, in other words, that the C.B.C. has made a projection, and all I am asking is that the projection be placed within the annual report so as to indicate the responsibilities.
Some hon. members may say, perhaps: "What about population shifts? If the C.B.C. is adjusting to population shifts the projection might not be reliable". Well, my experience is that the C.B.C. tends to wait for the dominion bureau of statistics; it waits for the census figures which come out at ten year intervals. So that is really not a valid objection.

I submit, too, that the C.B.C. very much needs to give us detailed projections. Do hon. members think we would have this CJBC fuss, with all the controvesy that has gone with it, if the corporation had been obliged to project this particular matter? I say this because it is a matter which involves a change in the service given across the country. This amendment does not deal with programs in any shape or form. It is concerned strictly with service extensions, and as I see service extensions, the term covers radio and television on both the English and the French networks. It means the international service. It has nothing to do with capital structures such as buildings in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto. But it does include anything to do with the extension of the service to more people, or with giving a variety of programs to more people. This means that in the corporation's tremendous desire to fulfil its mandate, for example to extend the French language and French language programs across the country, it would be required to append to its annual report a five year projection showing how it intended to do this, together with an estimate of the cost.
Obviously most members bring forward private members' bills because the area of interest is one which touches them very closely. Along with the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson), hon. members from areas such as Saguenay, and others in the north, I have been interested in the extension of services. We represent areas which, so far, are not served at all. How do we feel v/hen we hear about an extension to Edmonton where they already have television, or an extension to St. John's, where they already have a service, or about the conversion of CJBC to bring French to southern Ontario? These are all worthy things to do, but the point is that in the Toronto area people already have all manner of excellent radio and television services. There is television already in St. John's, Newfoundland. There is television in Edmonton. But there are parts of this country where it is still impossible to get television reception, and the C.B.C. is not moving very fast in fulfilling this portion of its mandate.
The C.B.C. tells us it has a formula. Yes, it has a formula, and it is a mysterious one; most of us have difficulty in figuring it out. The C.B.C. pleads poverty. Mr. Ouimet pleaded in 1960-61: We are doing our very, very best. But in the very next year the corporation handed $7 or $8 million back to the treasury, presumably as an example of how efficiently it was operating-"We don't really need to take up all the money that is provided in our budget". How can this be explained to the people who still do not enjoy radio or television coverage? Here we see the corporation

handing back government funds and, let us say, commercial revenue, at the same time as Mr. Ouimet and his followers are telling us they are doing their best for the people who still do not enjoy coverage.
Look at what is involved in the budget of $100 million or $110 million a year. Every member here knows that this is big money. One hundred million dollars is not to be sneezed at. Yet note the budget for extension of services. It is something over $1 million- up to $2 million. It really is pettiness. This is why I tend to become a little sceptical about this C.B.C. mandate, though some of my colleagues disagree with me here. I wonder how much the directors of the beloved corporation are really thinking about the Canadian population as a whole. Is it possible that they have got a metropolitan syndrome and see everything in terms of these great aggregations of people, these big market areas where it is possible to obtain commercial revenue and get a reception large enough to be able to say: These are your ratings? This is bound to be the suspicion, when one considers the small fraction of the budget which the C.B.C. sets aside to extend its services.
The corporation talks about the cost per head, and says: Oh dear, we have to move very carefully and wait until the next census to see how the population is growing. If the C.B.C. believes its mandate, it will take the necessary steps to provide service to 100 per cent of the Canadian people as soon as possible, before it begins providing secondary or tertiary services or other extensions and diversions to those people in Canada who are already covered. In this whole field of cultural entertainment there is not any question about it that a minority in this country is going short, and their complaint is that they are going short while they are paying for the service as general taxpayers.
The reason we would like this amendment to the bill and we know it would require the co-operation of the government, the treasury board associated with it, the C.B.C. and the board of broadcast governors, if they have any responsibility in supervising and directing the whole broadcasting policy-is to get complete broadcasting to the people.
The reason that we have a community antenna problem is because of the failure of the C.B.C. to move more quickly to extend service. This is one of the reasons why we have so much criticism of the C.B.C., particularly in the rural areas. It has moved too slowly to extend its services, but I am not going to suggest that there has been any favouritism in the extension of the services it has made.
