speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: NOTICE TO PARLIAMENT OF EXTENSIONS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has suggested that the bill now before us would really effect only a minor change in national broadcasting. On the face of the matter he is correct, but if we look at it a little more carefully we find

Broadcasting Act
that it raises in a most direct way the problem of the relationship between a crown corporation, such as the C.B.C. and parliament.
We want our national broadcasting service to be removed as far as possible from the shifting winds of political opinion. We believe it best that the corporation should not be rocked in its judgment by every favourable breeze or by every blast of denunciation. On the other hand I think we would all agree we do not wish the corporation to be wilful or capricious.
It is only realistic to remind ourselves that there is no such thing as a sure or foolproof arrangement by which we can accomplish both these ends. The result is that we balance them all rather uneasily in a tension one against the other. We have a certain arrangement, and the hon. member for Port Arthur has suggested that in general he values this arrangement. I would agree with him. That arrangement has worked reasonably well.
I do not wish to argue that the hon. member intends to disrupt the prevailing system; nor indeed will I argue that if this bill were to pass it would bring on vast disorders that the hon. member did not foresee, but I do want to explore some of the implications of the bill.
As the hon. member who introduced it suggested, the bill points to both the past and the future. First, it provides that the corporation shall append to its annual report particulars of each extension to the national broadcasting service within Canada that was undertaken or completed during that year, and shall show the cost thereof. Second, it provides that with its annual report the corporation will give particulars of each extension the corporation proposes to undertake, or to complete, during the five financial years next ensuing, together with a statement of the estimated cost thereof.
At first glance the provision concerning each extension during the previous fiscal year seems reasonable enough. It can be contended, and I think many of us would be inclined to contend, that the C.B.C., to a large extent, is spending public moneys, moneys voted by parliament, and that surely it is not too much to expect the corporation to make an accounting of that part of its annual expenses spent on network and transmitting facilities in the case of each new area serviced. But let us remember that by enacting such a requirement we would be exposing the corporation to a spate of invidious criticism. Indeed, we would be inviting invidious criticism of our national broadcasting system.
The corporation already serves most of the Canadian people. Fully 93 per cent of our people are already within range of at least one Canadian television station, and about

65 per cent do have a choice between or among Canadian stations. Those people who are not yet served live, as the hon. member pointed out, in sparsely populated areas, where the cost per capita of providing facilities inevitably is relatively high, and in some cases extremely high.
It is not always realized by all that the C.B.C. is no mere commercial venture, that it has a special role or function in the development of Canada's national culture and aspirations. If it is to perform this function it cannot be tested, especially when services are to be extended to the more sparsely populated areas of the country, by mere, normal, commercial standards. And this, the judging of these extensions by inappropriate commercial standards, is precisely what one might anticipate if this bill were to be enacted.
I had guessed, Mr. Speaker, that this bill was introduced because the hon. member wishes to hasten the extension of C.B.C. coverage in certain areas. He has confirmed the validity of my guess. I did not make this guess simply by ratiocination. I happen to come from a part of the country where we do not enjoy the best of television broadcasting, even though C.B.C. transmission passes directly through the area, so I know whereof he complains. But it would be unfortunate,
1	think, if the enactment he suggests had precisely the opposite effect to which he desires. I suspect there are people in the country-

Well, if it is improper now it would certainly be worse if the hon. member's bill passes. At page 224 of the report of the royal commission on broadcasting, made in 1957, there is the following sentence:
We also feel that, while no rigid line can be drawn, the cost of extending coverage beyond the level of 90 per cent of the population would not be justified, unless and until the Canadian population is substantially larger and more concentrated, or new technological developments in television reduce the costs of reaching scattered groups of people.
That the corporation has not been wasting time is shown by the fact previously mentioned, that at present 93 per cent of the people in this country are already within range of at least one Canadian television station.
The disadvantages of the second aspect of the bill-the provision for the publication by the corporation of particulars of each extension of the service proposed during the five financial years next ensuing-are more immediately obvious. As a framework for investigation, the corporation does maintain a moving five-year projection of service extensions either being considered or already in progress. The bill now before the house proposes that this projection be set forth in the annual report of the corporation.
If this projection were a plan, the bill might have some merit; but strictly speaking it is not a plan. Initially a highly tentative priority list of extensions is prepared, with the order of priority determined by the ratio of the population to be served to the money necessary to be expended to serve them. But the order of this tentative list will change, and a list published today I submit might be out of date within six months. First, when the physical characteristics of an area are examined and when quotations have been received, that area may be raised or lowered on the priority list. Moreover the cost factors may vary from year to year.
Second, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's plan, or projection-the latter is the more exact word-may be altered by the planning of private companies who may decide to erect stations or satellites. Third, an effort is made by the corporation to maintain some kind of equitable balance between extensions in the French language and extensions in the English language. It would hardly be appropriate, I submit-

Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly on this matter because I would like to see this bill come to a vote. I think that too often our private members' bills are frustrated, and I do not think they should be frustrated just because they are private members' bills. This bill introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has a great deal of merit. As so often happens, the people who put bills through parliament and set up crown corporations are not doing it, I think-and I will give the best interpretation that I can-in order to abdicate their duty to the Canadian people. Quite the contrary; they are setting

Broadcasting Act
up what they feel is efficient machinery for putting our will into operation. At no time- certainly I can speak for myself, and I think I speak for the average member of parliament-have we had any intention of giving up our interest in the matter merely by saying that such-and-such a corporation shall take on the responsibilities of running our transportation system, our mining for uranium, or our cultural media in the form of television.
The argument that 93 per cent of the people are already covered seems to me very specious, because the 7 per cent who are not covered-incidentally, in my own particular case, in Athabasca, perhaps 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the population are not covered -require T.V. a good deal more than do the people in the congested areas. If people in congested areas wish to go to a cultural medium, for instance an operetta, they just jump on the streetcar and go. The people in many parts of my district are hundreds of miles from any entertainment medium except radio, and I would argue that the 7 per cent who are not covered at the moment need television coverage a great deal more than the people in congested areas such as Edmonton, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. Our armed services boys who are out in far away places, often away from their families, would have a connection with their homes through television. They would know what is going on in the world and this would be the best medium possible. Therefore I do not think the percentage covered is much of an argument, either.
The fact that the C.B.C. might be forced to publish, or whatever you wish to call it, their plans or their policy is, I think, a very sound point, and certainly this is necessary so that parliament itself would know what our servants are doing. I think, in spite of the fact that they are crown corporations, they are still subject to the will of parliament as far as money is concerned, because we vote them very large sums of money and I think we cannot do our duty to the taxpayers, quite apart from those people who need coverage, unless we know just exactly what the corporation intends to do. Certainly we do not want to be patronized in any way by any crown corporation which is set up by us.
I should like to say a few words with regard to the cost involved. Over my desk every day come enormous amounts of literature, beautifully embossed. I do not know what is the cost of this literature, but a great many of the papers, and so on, that I receive contain nothing whatsoever that will assist me in bringing to the attention of this house very important items such as broadcasting and

television programs for our people. I think I have made my point, Mr. Speaker, that I thoroughly endorse the spirit of this bill. Perhaps it could be drafted in a little better fashion to please the feelings of those members of the corporation who may think we are overseeing them; but I think the spirit of the bill is that we will know what is intended and will be able to do more to assist this corporation in giving the people of Canada the T.V. coverage they desire. I must commend the hon. member for Port Arthur on what I think is one of the better private members' bills to be introduced this session.

Mr. Speaker, I have every sympathy for the case that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) made respecting the availability of television coverage to some of the outlying areas, because I happen to represent one of those constituencies where some people who are far back from the television broadcasting stations and satellites simply cannot receive this service. I am also convinced that for these people even one channel of television is more important than an extra channel being provided for the cities.
As the previous speaker has just pointed out, there are other, alternative forms of entertainment available to people in the cities, apart from television. I have every sympathy with the argument of the hon. member for Port Arthur, but I fail to see how he is going to correct that situation with this bill. It calls upon the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to give a five year projection of costs of extending programming. I believe that members of parliament have a right to know what are the financial prospects of the C.B.C., because after all we do vote public funds for that purpose. The hon. member for Port Arthur made it very clear that he was not talking about buildings and that sort of thing. I think we have the right to know about these things too. For example, we know that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are undertaking large, complex building structures in both Montreal and Toronto, and in the estimates for this year is an amount of something like $14 million for loans, and I suppose most of it will be used for this purpose. But when you vote $14 million on a $40 million or $50 million project, you are hooked-if I may put it that way-for the rest of it in future years.
I would remind the parliamentary secretary to the minister about this. He said it may be improper for the C.B.C. to make this kind of projection. It is equally improper for them to start on a building which they know very well they cannot finish with the amount of money that has been voted, because we

are not going to leave a building half erected, with the steel up, and then not allow it to be completed. Therefore that argument applies equally to the fact that the parliamentary secretary said it was improper for them to project their extension of programming.

Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before us tonight is of the utmost interest to me. I regret that the time allowed to me is so short for I would have many things to say on this matter. Nevertheless, since I should not like to be charged with killing this bill, I will limit myself to a few comments.
First, I should like to congratulate the mover of this bill. Even though I do not agree altogether with the entire contents of the bill, I agree nevertheless with the first part, which concerns the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's development.
As for the next point, that is for the C.B.C. to project its program of expansion for a five-year period, that might conflict with private enterprise and would in no way improve the situation even if projects were known in advance.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) spoke conservatively a while ago when he said that television services have cost a lot of money in certain districts. I should like to point out to him and to the house that in my own riding, one of the largest in Canada, Chibougamau and Chapais, two neighbouring mining towns which have a population of
13,000	to 14,000 are covered by television services.
The population is made up of miners, therefore of people whose average earnings are the highest in this country and who, consequently, are paying rather high taxes. To get T.V. services, these people have to pay $200 to get cable relay distribution, which is almost twice the amount referred to by the hon. member for Port Arthur; moreover, they have to pay a subscription fee of $6 per month, which has to be paid in advance.
I also wish to point out that these people are not given any guarantee upon signing their contract because, the person who is serving them at present does not guarantee

Broadcasting Act
that he will provide that service for one year, two years, five years or any other period of time.
You can well understand in what position these people find themselves just now. It is, therefore, important that they be served just as well as we are in the southern part of the county of Chapleau where private enterprise also serves the area.
I must also say that the area I represent is very well served and the service there is excellent. Considering that television is a recognized fact by everyone, that it has become a necessity, and especially that it is a medium of information and education, since we now have televised school programs, the people of these districts should benefit from it just as those from other regions.
So, I support the previous speakers who mentioned that those who are not served now by television services are precisely those who should be the first ones to enjoy them, because they live in more or less isolated areas and they have no other means of recreation, education, and information as far as television programs are concerned. According to my information, the C.B.C. is, I think ready to serve those areas, but there is always a financial problem. Then, it would be appropriate to recommend to the government to provide the C.B.C. with the necessary funds to serve all the areas they possibly can. I was assured that it was possible for the C.B.C. to serve every part of Canada. Consequently, the government only has to make financially possible what is physically feasible and everybody will be satisfied.

Mr. Speaker, obviously many things have already been said about the bill now before us. I would not want to repeat all the arguments put forward, but, for all that, I would not like you to forget their validity.
For instance, they spoke about geographical problems as well as the difficulties for the C.B.C. to balance the distribution of French and English broadcasting facilities. I do not think that this problem can be thrust aside even if it is as acute as that which exists at the present time in the Toronto area.
Therefore, I do not want to deal again with all the arguments that have been put forward. But I think that the bill now before us contains a few provisions which are incompatible with the present position of the C.B.C.
I am more particularly thinking of the second part and speaking from an accountant's
point of view. The C.B.C. operates on an annual budget, and if the corporation, which has to keep within the narrow limits of an annual budget were to be asked to establish a five-year projection of what it intends or will have to do, I think it would be impractical. Indeed, I doubt that the corporation would have any basis at all to do so, because it cannot foresee the possibilities or the generosity of parliament. Consequently, the corporation cannot suppose that it will be able to embark on such and such a project three or four years hence.
Moreover, having in mind all the arguments which have been put forward by the previous speakers, we all know that the situation may change, that a priority list which was, for instance, established this year, may be changed next year, on account of new factors, and that the corporation may have to prepare new projects.
Under the circumstances, I do not see how the C.B.C., given its yearly budget, could make a five-year projection in regard to the works it intends to undertake. The hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) evidently raised a very good argument, that of the areas which are not yet accessible to private radio or television. I think that if the C.B.C. divulged its program for the next five years, this would perhaps discourage private enterprise which might be interested, being alone to serve areas which up to now have not been covered, and to supply radio and television service to the population of these areas.
I think we should maintain a balance between public and private enterprise and we should not, ahead of time, close all avenues to private enterprise, discourage it systematically under the terms of an act. I think we should not publish in advance projections which might be inaccurate and never come true.
Personally, and with reservations-it is a personal opinion-I might accept the first part of this amendment, because parliament has to vote money to meet the expenditures of the C.B.C., and it is therefore only legitimate to examine and check them.
As for the second part, unless the hon. member for Port Arthur wishes to move an amendment, I do not see how I could commit, for the next five years-
